follow_up_questions: What is the difference between a Servlet Filter and a HandlerInterceptor?
How does Content Negotiation work in Spring MVC?

questions.question_title: How do you implement robust Global Exception Handling with @RestControllerAdvice and RFC 7807?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how to build a centralized error handling strategy using @RestControllerAdvice and @ExceptionHandler. How does Spring Boot 3 support RFC 7807 ProblemDetail?
expected_answer_points: @RestControllerAdvice combines @ControllerAdvice and @ResponseBody to intercept exceptions thrown by controllers globally.
@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class) captures validation failures and formats clean field-error arrays.
@ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class) maps domain errors to HTTP 404.
Generic @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) catches unhandled errors, logs stack traces securely, and returns 500 without leaking internal secrets.
Spring Boot 3 introduces ProblemDetail (RFC 7807): standardized JSON response with type, title, status, detail, instance, and custom properties.
questions.sample_answer: Create a class annotated with @RestControllerAdvice. Define methods with @ExceptionHandler for specific exceptions: MethodArgumentNotValidException to return field-level validation errors (HTTP 400), custom business exceptions (e.g. EntityNotFoundException -> HTTP 404), and a fallback Exception handler returning HTTP 500. In Spring Boot 3, return ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) to provide a standardized, machine-readable error format including status, detail, and timestamp.
follow_up_questions: What property in Spring Boot 3 enables automatic RFC 7807 ProblemDetail responses?
Why should you never expose internal exception messages or stack traces in HTTP 500 responses to clients?

questions.question_title: How does Bean Validation (@Valid, @Validated) work in Spring Boot?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how @Valid and @Validated trigger JSR-380 validation. Compare common constraints (@NotNull, @NotEmpty, @NotBlank, @Size, @Pattern) and explain validation groups.
expected_answer_points: @Valid (standard JSR-380) vs @Validated (Spring variant supporting validation groups).
@NotNull: Value must not be null (permits empty string '').
@NotEmpty: Not null and length/size > 0 (permits whitespace '   ').
@NotBlank: Not null, length > 0, and contains at least one non-whitespace character (strictly for CharSequences).
Validation groups allow applying different validation rules to the same DTO (e.g. CreateGroup vs UpdateGroup where ID is mandatory on update but omitted on create).
Custom validators: implement ConstraintValidator<MyAnnotation, TargetType>.
questions.sample_answer: Spring Boot Starter Validation brings Hibernate Validator. In controllers, annotate DTO parameters with @Valid or @Validated. @NotNull checks for null; @NotEmpty checks non-null and non-empty; @NotBlank checks non-null, non-empty, and non-whitespace. @Validated supports validation groups, allowing the same DTO to enforce required fields during POST /create while relaxing them for PATCH /update. Failures throw MethodArgumentNotValidException.
follow_up_questions: How do you validate path variables and query parameters on a @RestController?
How do you implement a custom cross-field validator (e.g. password matches confirmPassword)?

questions.question_title: What is Spring Boot Actuator, and how do you secure its production endpoints?
questions.question_prompt: Explain Actuator endpoints (/health, /info, /metrics, /env, /prometheus). How do you customize health indicators (HealthIndicator), configure liveness/readiness probes for Kubernetes, and secure sensitive actuator paths?
expected_answer_points: Actuator provides production monitoring endpoints: /health, /metrics, /env, /threaddump, /heapdump, /prometheus.
Kubernetes probes: management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true exposes /health/liveness (app running) and /health/readiness (ready to receive traffic).
Custom HealthIndicator: Implement HealthIndicator and override health() returning Health.up() or Health.down().withDetail().

Security: By default only /health is exposed over web. Never expose sensitive endpoints (/env, /beans) publicly; secure via Spring Security role (ADMIN) or bind management port to an internal private port (management.server.port=8081).
questions.sample_answer: Actuator exposes operational endpoints for monitoring application health and metrics. In Kubernetes, it provides dedicated /health/liveness and /health/readiness probes. You can add custom health checks by implementing HealthIndicator (e.g. checking 3rd party API connectivity). In production, sensitive endpoints like /env or /heapdump should never be exposed publicly: either restrict management.endpoints.web.exposure.include to health,info, or place actuator on an internal port protected by Spring Security.
follow_up_questions: How does Micrometer integrate with Spring Boot Actuator to export metrics to Prometheus?
What is the difference between a Liveness failure and a Readiness failure in Kubernetes?

questions.question_title: Compare @SpringBootTest, @WebMvcTest, and @DataJpaTest in Spring Boot testing.
questions.question_prompt: Explain test slice annotations in Spring Boot. Why should you prefer sliced tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) over full @SpringBootTest for unit and integration testing?
expected_answer_points: @SpringBootTest: Loads the entire ApplicationContext and all beans. Heavy and slow; ideal for end-to-end integration tests.
@WebMvcTest: Slices the web layer only (controllers, filters, HandlerInterceptors). Mocks the service/repository layer using @MockBean. Fast controller testing with MockMvc.

@DataJpaTest: Slices the persistence layer only (entities, Spring Data repositories, TestEntityManager). Configures an embedded or test database, runs tests in transactions that roll back automatically.
@MockBean / @MockitoBean: Injects a Mockito mock directly into the Spring ApplicationContext for sliced testing.
questions.sample_answer: @SpringBootTest starts the entire application context, making tests thorough but slow. Test slicing allows testing isolated layers: @WebMvcTest boots only MVC components (controllers, validation, filters) while mocking services with @MockBean, enabling fast API contract tests. @DataJpaTest boots only JPA entities and repositories with an in-memory/test database and automatic transaction rollback after every test method.
follow_up_questions: What is Testcontainers and why is it preferred over H2 for @DataJpaTest integration tests?
What replaces @MockBean in Spring Boot 3.4+ (@MockitoBean)?

questions.question_title: Compare @Value and @ConfigurationProperties for external configuration binding.
questions.question_prompt: Why is type-safe @ConfigurationProperties preferred over @Value for complex application settings? Discuss validation, relaxed binding, and constructor binding with records.
expected_answer_points: @Value injects individual property values using SpEL (${app.timeout:5000}). Drawbacks: error-prone strings, no type hierarchy, difficult to validate grouped configurations.
@ConfigurationProperties binds a hierarchical group of properties (e.g. prefix = 'app.security') to a strongly-typed Java POJO or Java Record.
Relaxed binding: accepts kebab-case (max-retry), camelCase (maxRetry), or UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (MAX_RETRY) interchangeably.
Supports JSR-380 validation (@Validated on the class with @Min, @NotBlank).
Constructor binding with Java 17+ Records enables immutable configuration classes.
questions.sample_answer: @Value injects single values with SpEL expressions, but lacks structure, grouping, and compile-time validation. @ConfigurationProperties provides type-safe hierarchical binding to POJOs or Java 17 Records. It supports relaxed binding (kebab-case in YAML matches camelCase in Java), enables validation via @Validated annotations, and generates IDE autocompletion metadata via spring-boot-configuration-processor.
follow_up_questions: How do you bind a List or Map of objects using @ConfigurationProperties?
What dependency generates IDE metadata for custom @ConfigurationProperties?

questions.question_title: How do you implement Distributed Tracing and MDC logging in Spring Boot microservices?
questions.question_prompt: Explain Mapped Diagnostic Context (MDC) in SLF4J/Logback. How do Micrometer Tracing and OpenTelemetry propagate traceId and spanId across HTTP and Kafka calls?
expected_answer_points: MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) is a thread-local map provided by SLF4J that attaches contextual key-values (e.g. userId, traceId) to all log lines generated by that thread.
TraceId uniquely identifies an entire user request lifecycle across distributed microservices; SpanId identifies work within a single service.
Micrometer Tracing (replacing Spring Cloud Sleuth in Boot 3) automatically generates traceId/spanId and injects them into MDC.
Propagation: HTTP headers (W3C traceparent or B3 headers) and Kafka message headers transmit trace context between services.
Async thread issue: Because MDC is ThreadLocal, trace context is lost when offloading to @Async thread pools unless using a TaskDecorator to copy MDC context.
questions.sample_answer: MDC stores key-value pairs (like traceId, userId) in thread-local storage so Logback prints them in every log pattern. In microservices, Micrometer Tracing generates a unique traceId and injects it into MDC. When invoking another service, it propagates the traceId via HTTP headers (traceparent) or Kafka headers. Downstream services read the header and populate their own MDC, allowing all logs across distributed systems to be correlated in tools like Grafana Loki or ELK.
follow_up_questions: How do you propagate MDC context into @Async executor worker threads?
What is the difference between Micrometer Tracing and Spring Cloud Sleuth?

questions.question_title: How do you handle long-running asynchronous HTTP requests in Spring Boot?
questions.question_prompt: Compare DeferredResult, CompletableFuture, and Server-Sent Events (SseEmitter) in Spring MVC controllers. How do they release Tomcat container threads while waiting for long I/O?
expected_answer_points: Synchronous blocking: A Tomcat worker thread is occupied for the entire duration of the request, exhausting the connection pool during slow third-party calls.
CompletableFuture<ResponseEntity<T>>: Controller returns future immediately; Tomcat thread is returned to the pool while worker pool computes the result.
DeferredResult<T>: Managed asynchronous result. Any external event or thread can complete the DeferredResult by calling .setResult(), unblocking the client response.
SseEmitter: Keeps HTTP connection open for one-way streaming of events from server to client over a single connection.
Async support requires configuring WebMvcConfigurer.configureAsyncSupport().
questions.sample_answer: Returning CompletableFuture<T> or DeferredResult<T> releases the Tomcat container thread immediately back to the pool while the long-running operation executes on a separate background thread pool. Once the future completes or deferredResult.setResult() is called, the servlet container dispatches the response to the client. This prevents Tomcat worker thread exhaustion during slow I/O or external API calls.
follow_up_questions: What timeout configuration is required when using DeferredResult?
What is the difference between SseEmitter and WebSockets for real-time data?

questions.question_title: How does Graceful Shutdown work in Spring Boot?
questions.question_prompt: Explain server.shutdown=graceful. What happens to active in-flight requests and incoming requests when a SIGTERM signal is received in containerized environments?
expected_answer_points: Configured via server.shutdown=graceful in application.properties.
Upon receiving SIGTERM, the embedded web server stops accepting new connections immediately.
Existing in-flight requests are allowed a grace period (spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, default 30s) to complete.
If requests complete within grace period, JVM terminates cleanly; if timeout expires, active requests are forcefully terminated.
In Kubernetes, paired with preStop sleep hooks to allow ingress load balancers to remove the pod before shutdown begins.
questions.sample_answer: Setting server.shutdown=graceful ensures that when Kubernetes sends a SIGTERM, the embedded web server (Tomcat) stops accepting new incoming traffic while giving active in-flight requests up to 30 seconds (configurable via timeout-per-shutdown-phase) to finish processing cleanly. This prevents dropped HTTP requests and incomplete database writes during rolling deployments.
follow_up_questions: Why is a preStop sleep hook recommended in Kubernetes pod spec alongside graceful shutdown?
How are background @Scheduled tasks and ThreadPoolExecutors gracefully terminated?

questions.question_title: How do you create a custom Spring Boot Starter library?
questions.question_prompt: Walk through creating a custom reusable Spring Boot Starter: naming conventions, pom.xml structure, AutoConfiguration class, @ConfigurationProperties, and registering in AutoConfiguration.imports.
expected_answer_points: Naming rule: Third-party starters must NOT start with spring-boot-starter-*; use myfeature-spring-boot-starter.
Module structure: typically split into myfeature-spring-boot-autoconfigure (code) and myfeature-spring-boot-starter (empty dependency aggregator).
Define @ConfigurationProperties class for customizable properties.
Define @AutoConfiguration class with conditional checks (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean).
Register the auto-configuration class in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports.
questions.sample_answer: To build a custom starter, create an autoconfigure module with an @AutoConfiguration class annotated with @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean, backed by an @ConfigurationProperties class. Register the class in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports. Package it under a name like myproject-spring-boot-starter so consuming applications can simply include the dependency and have beans automatically configured.
follow_up_questions: Why shouldn't third-party starters use the spring-boot-starter-* prefix?
How do you write unit tests for custom auto-configurations using ApplicationContextRunner?

questions.question_title: How do you configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) in Spring Boot?
questions.question_prompt: Compare @CrossOrigin annotation at controller level with global WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings() and CorsFilter. Why does Spring Security sometimes block CORS pre-flight OPTIONS requests before Spring MVC handles them?
expected_answer_points: @CrossOrigin: Fine-grained, declared on controller class or method. Hard to maintain globally across enterprise APIs.
WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings(): Global configuration across URL patterns.

Spring Security conflict: Spring Security filter chain runs BEFORE Spring MVC DispatcherServlet. If Security does not explicitly allow OPTIONS preflight requests or configure cors(), the preflight fails with 401/403.
Proper security fix: http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) in SecurityFilterChain, backed by a CorsConfigurationSource bean defining allowed origins, methods, and headers.
questions.sample_answer: CORS can be configured per-controller with @CrossOrigin or globally via WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings(). However, in applications using Spring Security, browser pre-flight OPTIONS requests hit the Security filter chain before Spring MVC is reached. If not configured, Spring Security rejects OPTIONS requests with 401/403. The correct solution is configuring http.cors() in SecurityFilterChain with a dedicated CorsConfigurationSource bean specifying allowed origins, headers, and HTTP methods.
follow_up_questions: What headers does a browser send during an HTTP OPTIONS pre-flight request?
Why is allowCredentials(true) incompatible with allowedOrigins('*')?

questions.subtopic: Spring Boot Docker Layering & Native Images
questions.question_title: How do layered JARs and GraalVM Native Images optimize container deployments in Spring Boot 3?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how Spring Boot's layered JAR feature speeds up Docker container builds. What are GraalVM Native Images (Ahead-of-Time compilation) and their benefits/trade-offs?
expected_answer_points: Layered JARs: Separates fat JAR into 4 layers: dependencies, spring-boot-loader, snapshot-dependencies, and application code.

Docker caching: In Dockerfiles, copying dependencies first and application code last ensures dependency layers are cached when only business code changes, reducing image build/push time from minutes to seconds.
GraalVM Native Image: Compiles Java bytecode directly into a standalone platform-native machine binary via Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) compilation.
Benefits: Instant startup (milliseconds) and tiny memory footprint (tens of MBs).
Trade-offs: Long compilation times, closed-world assumption (reflection, dynamic proxies, and JNI require AOT reachability metadata hints).
questions.sample_answer: Spring Boot layered JARs split a fat JAR into dependencies, loader, snapshots, and application layers. In a multi-stage Docker build, copying dependencies before application code leverages Docker layer caching so re-building an image only pushes changed application classes. In Spring Boot 3, GraalVM AOT compilation builds standalone native binaries that start in milliseconds with minimal RAM, ideal for serverless or scale-to-zero workloads, at the cost of longer build times and requiring AOT hints for dynamic reflection.
follow_up_questions: How does the Spring AOT engine generate reflection configuration for GraalVM?
Why is dynamic class loading unsupported in GraalVM native images?

questions.question_title: How does the Spring Security Filter Chain work internally?
questions.question_prompt: Explain DelegatingFilterProxy, FilterChainProxy, SecurityFilterChain, and the sequence of key security filters (SecurityContextPersistenceFilter/SecurityContextHolderFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter, AuthorizationFilter).
expected_answer_points: DelegatingFilterProxy: Standard Servlet Filter registered in web.xml / servlet container that delegates doFilter calls to a Spring-managed bean named 'springSecurityFilterChain'.
FilterChainProxy: Master filter that contains one or more SecurityFilterChain instances matched by request matchers.
SecurityFilterChain: List of security filters executed in defined order.
SecurityContextHolderFilter: Restores SecurityContext from SecurityContextRepository into SecurityContextHolder.
Authentication filters (e.g. UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter): Extract credentials and invoke AuthenticationManager.
ExceptionTranslationFilter: Catches AuthenticationException (triggers AuthenticationEntryPoint / 401) and AccessDeniedException (triggers AccessDeniedHandler / 403).
AuthorizationFilter (formerly FilterSecurityInterceptor): Enforces authorization rules using AuthorizationManager.
questions.sample_answer: Servlet requests enter DelegatingFilterProxy, which delegates to FilterChainProxy. FilterChainProxy matches the request to a SecurityFilterChain. SecurityContextHolderFilter restores existing authentication. Custom or built-in authentication filters validate credentials and populate SecurityContextHolder. Next, ExceptionTranslationFilter acts as an exception barrier. Finally, AuthorizationFilter checks whether the authenticated user has permissions; if rejected, ExceptionTranslationFilter catches the error and invokes AuthenticationEntryPoint (401) or AccessDeniedHandler (403).
follow_up_questions: Why was SecurityContextPersistenceFilter replaced by SecurityContextHolderFilter in Spring Security 6?
How do you inspect the exact list and order of filters running in your SecurityFilterChain?

questions.question_title: Explain the roles of AuthenticationManager, AuthenticationProvider, and UserDetailsService.
questions.question_prompt: Walk through how Spring Security processes an authentication attempt: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken, AuthenticationManager (ProviderManager), DaoAuthenticationProvider, UserDetailsService, and PasswordEncoder.
expected_answer_points: Authentication object: Represents the user; holds principal, credentials, authorities, and isAuthenticated boolean.
AuthenticationManager: Primary API for authentication. The standard implementation is ProviderManager.
ProviderManager delegates to a list of AuthenticationProviders: each provider checks if it supports the specific Authentication token type.
DaoAuthenticationProvider: Standard provider that calls UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername() to fetch stored UserDetails.
PasswordEncoder.matches(): Compares plain-text submitted password against stored BCrypt hash.
If matched, creates a fully authenticated Authentication token (with credentials cleared) stored in SecurityContextHolder.
questions.sample_answer: A login filter constructs an unauthenticated UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken and passes it to AuthenticationManager (ProviderManager). ProviderManager iterates registered AuthenticationProviders. DaoAuthenticationProvider handles it by calling UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername() to retrieve user details from the database. It then uses PasswordEncoder.matches() to verify the submitted password against the BCrypt hash. If valid, an authenticated token populated with GrantedAuthorities is returned and stored in SecurityContextHolder.
follow_up_questions: What happens if multiple AuthenticationProviders are configured in ProviderManager?
Why should you never write your own raw password comparison and always use PasswordEncoder.matches()?

questions.question_title: How do you implement a stateless JWT Authentication Filter in Spring Security 6?
questions.question_prompt: Describe building a custom OncePerRequestFilter for JWT validation: extracting the Bearer token, parsing and verifying signature, setting up SecurityContext, and configuring SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS in SecurityFilterChain.
expected_answer_points: Create a filter extending OncePerRequestFilter (guarantees execution once per request dispatch).
Extract Authorization header: check for 'Bearer ' prefix.
Validate JWT: verify HMAC or RSA signature, verify expiration date, extract username and roles/claims.
If valid and SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() is null, construct UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken with principal and authorities.
Set details via WebAuthenticationDetailsSource and update SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(authToken).
FilterChain configuration: http.sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS)) and addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class).
questions.sample_answer: Extend OncePerRequestFilter to intercept requests before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter. Extract the 'Bearer ' token from the Authorization header. Verify the cryptographic signature and expiration with a JWT parser. Extract the username and authorities, construct a UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken, and store it in SecurityContextHolder. In the SecurityFilterChain bean, set SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS so Spring Security creates no HTTP sessions, and disable CSRF.
follow_up_questions: Why must CSRF protection be disabled when using pure stateless Bearer JWT authentication?
What happens if the JWT is expired, and how should the filter respond?

questions.question_title: How does BCryptPasswordEncoder work, and why is salt generation built-in?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how BCrypt hashes passwords. What is the salt, what is the work factor (strength), and why does hashing the exact same password twice produce two completely different hash strings?
expected_answer_points: BCrypt is an adaptive cryptographic hash function based on the Blowfish cipher.
Built-in Salt: BCrypt generates a random 16-byte salt for every hash and encodes it directly into the output string ($2a$10$...).
Because each hash uses a fresh random salt, hashing the same password twice yields different strings, defeating rainbow table attacks.
Work factor (cost, default 10): Defines 2^cost hashing rounds. It is computationally expensive by design to resist brute-force hardware/GPU cracking.

PasswordEncoder.matches(raw, hash) extracts the embedded salt from the stored hash, hashes the raw password with that salt, and compares results using constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks.
questions.sample_answer: BCrypt is an adaptive slow hash designed to thwart GPU brute-force cracking. It generates a unique random 16-byte salt for every password and embeds the algorithm version, work factor (cost), and salt directly inside the resulting string. Because the salt is randomized on each hash, the same password produces different hashes every time. When checking matches(), BCrypt extracts the salt from the stored hash, applies the same rounds to the candidate password, and verifies them in constant time.
follow_up_questions: What is Argon2 and how does it compare with BCrypt?
What is a timing attack and how does MessageDigest.isEqual prevent it?

questions.question_title: How does Method-Level Security work with @PreAuthorize and @EnableMethodSecurity?
questions.question_prompt: Explain @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @PreFilter, and @PostFilter. How does SpEL allow fine-grained access control such as checking #id against authentication.name?
expected_answer_points: Enabled via @EnableMethodSecurity (replaces legacy @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6).

@PreAuthorize: Evaluates SpEL expression BEFORE method invocation (e.g. @PreAuthorize('hasRole("ADMIN") or #userId == authentication.principal.id')). If false, throws AccessDeniedException without executing method.
@PostAuthorize: Evaluates expression AFTER method completes; can inspect returnObject (e.g. returnObject.owner == authentication.name).
@PreFilter and @PostFilter: Filter collection arguments or returned collections based on ownership rules.
Operates via Spring AOP proxies around annotated service methods.
questions.sample_answer: Annotating a configuration class with @EnableMethodSecurity enables AOP proxies on service methods. @PreAuthorize evaluates a SpEL expression before execution; for example, @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #id == authentication.principal.id") ensures only administrators or the resource owner can invoke the method. @PostAuthorize checks the returned object (returnObject) after execution, aborting with AccessDeniedException if the rule fails.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between hasRole('ADMIN') and hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN')?
Why doesn't @PreAuthorize work when calling another method within the same service bean?

questions.question_title: What is Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), and how does Spring Security defend against it?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how CSRF attacks exploit ambient browser credentials (cookies). How does the Synchronizer Token Pattern (CsrfFilter) work, and when is it safe to disable CSRF?
expected_answer_points: CSRF attack: A malicious site tricks a victim's browser into executing an unwanted action on an authenticated application where the user has an active session cookie (browsers automatically attach session cookies to cross-origin requests).

Defense: Synchronizer Token Pattern. The server generates a random, cryptographically secure token tied to the session. Mutating requests (POST, PUT, DELETE) must provide this token via header (X-XSRF-TOKEN) or hidden form parameter.
CsrfFilter: Validates token on mutating methods; rejects mismatches with 403 Forbidden.

Safe to disable: Only when building stateless REST APIs authenticated purely via Bearer tokens in headers (not stored in cookies), because browsers do not automatically attach Authorization headers across origins.
questions.sample_answer: CSRF occurs when a malicious website tricks a user's browser into submitting requests to another site where the user is logged in, exploiting automatic browser cookie transmission. Spring Security defends against this with CsrfFilter using the Synchronizer Token Pattern: every mutating request must include a random CSRF token generated by the server. CSRF can only be safely disabled in stateless REST APIs where authentication uses custom headers (like Authorization: Bearer) rather than ambient browser session cookies.
follow_up_questions: What is the SameSite cookie attribute (Strict/Lax/None) and does it eliminate the need for CSRF tokens?
How do Single Page Applications (React/Angular) handle CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse()?

questions.question_title: How is SecurityContext stored, and what happens in multi-threaded asynchronous tasks?
questions.question_prompt: Explain SecurityContextHolder strategy: MODE_THREADLOCAL vs MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL vs MODE_GLOBAL. How do you propagate security context to @Async methods or custom thread pools?
expected_answer_points: Default strategy: SecurityContextHolder.MODE_THREADLOCAL (each thread maintains its own isolated SecurityContext).
Problem: Worker threads created by custom ExecutorService or @Async do not inherit the calling thread's SecurityContext.
MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL: Automatically copies context to child threads when spawned, but fails in thread-pooling scenarios where threads are reused.
Solution in Spring: DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor / DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService wraps executors and propagates context per task.
SecurityContextHolder.clearContext(): Mandatory cleanup in finally blocks to avoid memory leaks or context bleeding in pooled server threads.
questions.sample_answer: SecurityContextHolder defaults to MODE_THREADLOCAL, storing authentication in the current thread. In asynchronous workflows (@Async or thread pools), worker threads do not share this thread-local context. While MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL copies context to newly spawned threads, it breaks with pooled worker threads. The production solution is wrapping thread pools in DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService, which captures the caller's SecurityContext and attaches it to the worker thread for the duration of the task.
follow_up_questions: Why must SecurityContextHolder.clearContext() be called when a request completes?
How does DelegatingSecurityContextRunnable propagate credentials?

questions.question_title: How do you implement secure Refresh Token Rotation and Revocation?
questions.question_prompt: Design a secure token architecture using short-lived Access Tokens and long-lived Refresh Tokens. Explain Refresh Token Rotation and how to detect refresh token reuse attacks.
expected_answer_points: Access Token: Short lifespan (15 minutes); stateless JWT; used on every API call.
Refresh Token: Longer lifespan (7 days); stored in database with family ID and hashed token value; transmitted in secure httpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie.
Rotation mechanism: When the client calls /auth/refresh, the server invalidates the used refresh token and issues both a new access token and a brand-new refresh token.
Reuse detection: If a revoked refresh token is presented, it indicates token theft. The server immediately revokes the ENTIRE token family for that user session, forcing re-authentication.
Revocation: Logout deletes the refresh token record from database or marks it revoked in Redis blacklist.
questions.sample_answer: Issue short-lived access tokens (15m) for API calls and long-lived refresh tokens (7d) stored securely in HttpOnly cookies and tracked in a database. With Refresh Token Rotation, each refresh request consumes the old refresh token and issues a new pair. If a client attempts to refresh using an already-consumed token, the system detects a token reuse attack (theft) and immediately revokes all tokens in that user session family, forcing the user to re-login.
follow_up_questions: Where should the refresh token be stored on the client side to prevent XSS attacks?
How do you handle race conditions when two concurrent frontend requests attempt to rotate the same refresh token?

questions.question_title: What is the difference between AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how Spring Security distinguishes unauthenticated requests (HTTP 401) from unauthorized requests (HTTP 403). How do you customize AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler in Spring Security 6?
expected_answer_points: AuthenticationEntryPoint handles AuthenticationException (user is NOT logged in or token is invalid/missing). Returns HTTP 401 Unauthorized.
AccessDeniedHandler handles AccessDeniedException (user IS logged in, but lacks required role/authority). Returns HTTP 403 Forbidden.
Both are configured on ExceptionHandlingConfigurer: http.exceptionHandling(e -> e.authenticationEntryPoint(customEntryPoint).accessDeniedHandler(customDeniedHandler)).
Custom implementations write JSON error DTO directly to HttpServletResponse using Jackson ObjectMapper.
questions.sample_answer: AuthenticationEntryPoint is triggered when an unauthenticated user attempts to access a protected resource, returning HTTP 401 Unauthorized (e.g. invalid or missing JWT). AccessDeniedHandler is triggered when an authenticated user attempts an action for which they lack permissions, returning HTTP 403 Forbidden. Both are customized by implementing their respective interfaces and configuring them in http.exceptionHandling() to return clean JSON error payloads.
follow_up_questions: Why doesn't @RestControllerAdvice catch AuthenticationException thrown inside security filters?
How do you delegate security filter exceptions to HandlerExceptionResolver?

questions.question_title: How do you configure Spring Security as an OAuth2 Resource Server with JWT?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how to configure an application as an OAuth2 Resource Server using spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server and jwk-set-uri. How does JwtAuthenticationConverter map custom claims to GrantedAuthorities?
expected_answer_points: Include dependency: spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server.
Configuration: spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri=https://auth-server/.well-known/jwks.json.
SecurityFilterChain: http.oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())).
Spring automatically verifies incoming bearer tokens against the public keys fetched from the JWKS endpoint.
Custom claims mapping: By default Spring maps 'scope'/'scp' claims to 'SCOPE_' authorities. Custom JwtAuthenticationConverter extracts custom 'roles' claims and prepends 'ROLE_' prefix.
questions.sample_answer: Using spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server, point spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri to the identity provider's JWKS endpoint (e.g. Keycloak or Auth0). In SecurityFilterChain, call http.oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt()). Spring automatically fetches and caches public keys to verify signatures. Use a custom JwtAuthenticationConverter to map specific token claims (such as realm_access.roles) into Spring Security's GrantedAuthority objects with the 'ROLE_' prefix.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between symmetric (HMAC) and asymmetric (RSA/ECDSA) JWT signing in enterprise architectures?
How does JWKS caching and key rotation work?

questions.question_title: How does Spring Security prevent Session Fixation and enforce Concurrent Session Control?
questions.question_prompt: What is a Session Fixation attack? Explain how Spring Security's session fixation protection (changeSessionId) works and how to limit a user to at most 1 active concurrent session.
expected_answer_points: Session fixation: An attacker acquires a valid session ID, tricks the victim into logging in with that ID, and hijacks the authenticated session.
Protection: Upon successful authentication, Spring creates a new session ID while preserving attributes (sessionManagement.sessionFixation().changeSessionId()).
Concurrent session control: sessionManagement.maximumSessions(1).maxSessionsPreventsLogin(true or false).
Requires registering HttpSessionEventPublisher bean in Spring context so Spring Security tracks session destruction events.
If maxSessionsPreventsLogin=false, the previous session is invalidated (expired); if true, new login attempts are rejected.
questions.sample_answer: Session fixation occurs when an attacker forces a victim to use an attacker-known session ID that becomes authenticated. Spring Security defends against this by calling changeSessionId() upon authentication, issuing a brand-new session identifier while keeping user attributes. To restrict users to one concurrent session, configure maximumSessions(1) and register an HttpSessionEventPublisher bean so Spring tracks active sessions across logins and expirations.
follow_up_questions: Why must HttpSessionEventPublisher be registered in the Spring context for session limits to work?
How do distributed session stores like Spring Session with Redis handle concurrent session tracking?

questions.question_title: Explain the four Entity Lifecycle States in JPA: Transient, Persistent, Detached, and Removed.
questions.question_prompt: Walk through the four JPA entity states. What operations transition entities between them (persist, find, merge, remove, detach, clear)? What is the Persistence Context (First-Level Cache)?
expected_answer_points: 1. Transient (New): Instantiated with 'new'; has no database identifier (@Id) and is not associated with any persistence context.
2. Persistent (Managed): Associated with an active Persistence Context and has a database identity. Any field changes are automatically tracked (Dirty Checking) and synchronized on flush.
3. Detached: Has a database identity, but its Persistence Context closed or it was detached via em.detach() or em.clear(). Field modifications are not tracked unless merged.
4. Removed: Scheduled for deletion; DELETE statement will execute on flush.
Persistence Context acts as First-Level Cache: guarantees repeatable reads of entity instances within a transaction.
questions.sample_answer: JPA entities have 4 states: Transient (newly created in memory, not in DB or session), Persistent/Managed (tracked by the Persistence Context with a DB ID, where changes trigger automatic dirty checking), Detached (previously managed but the session closed; changes are untracked), and Removed (marked for SQL DELETE on transaction flush). Transitions occur via persist() [Transient->Managed], detach()/clear() [Managed->Detached], merge() [Detached->Managed], and remove() [Managed->Removed].
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between em.persist() and em.merge()?
Why doesn't calling a setter on a Managed entity require an explicit repository.save() call?

questions.question_title: What is the N+1 Query Problem in Hibernate, and what are 4 ways to resolve it?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how the N+1 query problem occurs with @OneToMany and @ManyToOne relationships. Detail 4 distinct solutions: JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, Batch Size (@BatchSize), and DTO projections.
expected_answer_points: Occurrence: Loading N parent entities causes 1 query for parents, then accessing a lazy association on each triggers N additional queries, resulting in 1 + N total queries.
Solution 1: JOIN FETCH in JPQL (SELECT p FROM Parent p JOIN FETCH p.children) loads parents and children in a single SQL query.
Solution 2: @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {'children'}) dynamically specifies fetch graphs without modifying JPQL.
Solution 3: @BatchSize(size = 50) or default_batch_fetch_size: Hibernate batches lazy queries using SQL IN (...), reducing N queries to N/50.
Solution 4: DTO projection: Select only required fields directly into a constructor expression (new com.dto.OrderSummary(...)), bypassing entity loading entirely.
questions.sample_answer: The N+1 problem occurs when fetching a collection of N parent entities triggers 1 initial query, and traversing a lazy association on each child generates N additional SQL queries (1+N total). Solutions include: 1) JPQL JOIN FETCH to join and fetch relations in a single query; 2) @EntityGraph to override fetching dynamically; 3) @BatchSize or default_batch_fetch_size to load lazy relationships in batches using SQL WHERE IN (...); and 4) Constructor DTO projections to select only necessary columns directly.
follow_up_questions: Why does using JOIN FETCH with multiple @OneToMany child collections cause MultipleBagFetchException?
How does pagination behave when combined with JOIN FETCH on a @OneToMany relationship?

questions.question_title: Why does LazyInitializationException happen, and how do you prevent it?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how Hibernate implements lazy loading using CGLIB/ByteBuddy dynamic proxies. What causes LazyInitializationException: 'could not initialize proxy - no Session', and why is Open Session in View (OSIV) an anti-pattern?
expected_answer_points: Hibernate creates dynamic bytecode proxies for lazy associations.
The proxy intercepts getter calls and queries the database using the active Persistence Context / Session.
If the transaction / Session commits and closes in the service layer, accessing an uninitialized lazy property in the controller or serialization layer throws LazyInitializationException.
Why Open Session in View (OSIV) is bad: It keeps database connections held open through the entire HTTP request rendering phase, exhausting connection pools and hiding N+1 queries.
Proper fix: Fetch required relationships within the transactional boundary using JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or DTO projections.
questions.sample_answer: Lazy relationships are represented by Hibernate proxies. When a getter is called outside an active transaction (such as in a controller or Jackson serializer after the service method returned), the session is already closed and Hibernate throws LazyInitializationException. Open Session in View (OSIV) keeps the DB connection open across the entire web request, which masks lazy queries and starves connection pools. The proper solution is fetching required data inside the service transaction using JOIN FETCH or DTO projections.
follow_up_questions: Why is FetchType.EAGER considered an anti-pattern for @ManyToOne and @OneToMany mappings?
What property disables Open Session in View in Spring Boot?

questions.question_title: Explain @Transactional: Propagation levels, rollback rules, and readOnly optimization.
questions.question_prompt: Compare REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, and NESTED transaction propagation. Why does @Transactional not roll back by default on checked exceptions, and what does readOnly = true do at the JDBC/Hibernate level?
expected_answer_points: REQUIRED (default): Joins existing transaction or creates a new one if none exists.
REQUIRES_NEW: Suspends existing transaction and starts an independent physical transaction. Errors in the new transaction do not roll back the outer transaction if caught.
NESTED: Executes within a nested transaction using database savepoints.
Rollback rule: By default, Spring rolls back ONLY on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error). To roll back on checked exceptions, declare @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class).
readOnly = true: Sets FlushMode.MANUAL in Hibernate (disables dirty checking, saving CPU and memory) and sets connection read-only on JDBC driver.
questions.sample_answer: Propagation defines transactional boundaries: REQUIRED joins an active transaction or creates one; REQUIRES_NEW suspends the current transaction to run an independent transaction (useful for audit logging). By default, Spring only rolls back on RuntimeException; checked exceptions must be explicitly specified with rollbackFor = Exception.class. Setting readOnly = true optimizes performance by disabling Hibernate dirty checking and allowing read-replica database routing.
follow_up_questions: What happens if a method annotated with @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) is called from another method within the same bean?
What is the difference between NESTED propagation and REQUIRES_NEW?

questions.question_title: Compare Optimistic Locking and Pessimistic Locking in JPA with real-world scenarios.
questions.question_prompt: When should you use @Version (Optimistic Locking) vs LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE (Pessimistic Locking)? What SQL is generated, and how do you handle OptimisticLockException?
expected_answer_points: Optimistic Locking: Assumes low conflict. Uses a @Version column (integer or timestamp). SQL: UPDATE tbl SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?.
If rows updated is 0 (someone else modified it first), JPA throws OptimisticLockException. Best for read-heavy workflows; handle by retrying transaction.
Pessimistic Locking: Assumes high contention. Uses database-level row locks: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE).
Blocks concurrent transactions until the current transaction commits or rolls back.
Best for critical financial debits or inventory reservations with high concurrent updates, but risks database deadlocks if not ordered carefully.
questions.sample_answer: Optimistic locking (@Version) does not lock database rows; on update, it verifies that the version in the DB matches the version read into memory. If another transaction updated the row in between, it throws OptimisticLockException, which can be retried. It is best for low-contention web apps. Pessimistic locking (LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) issues SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, acquiring a physical row lock in the database. It prevents race conditions during high-contention operations like banking debits, but reduces concurrency.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between PESSIMISTIC_READ and PESSIMISTIC_WRITE?
How do you configure a lock timeout for pessimistic queries to avoid hanging transactions?

questions.question_title: How do you properly map a bidirectional @OneToMany / @ManyToOne relationship in JPA?
questions.question_prompt: Explain the role of mappedBy, cascade types (CascadeType.ALL), orphanRemoval = true, and helper synchronization methods (addChild/removeChild). Why is @ManyToOne the owning side?
expected_answer_points: The side containing the foreign key in the database table is ALWAYS the owning side (@ManyToOne).
mappedBy belongs on the inverse side (@OneToMany) and references the field name on the owning entity.
CascadeType.ALL propagates persistence operations (persist, merge, remove) from parent to children.
orphanRemoval = true: Deleting a child from the parent's collection issues a DELETE statement for that child in the DB.
Helper methods: Must synchronize both sides in memory (e.g. this.items.add(item); item.setOrder(this);) to avoid inconsistent cache states.
questions.sample_answer: The @ManyToOne entity holds the foreign key and is the owning side. The @OneToMany side is the inverse side and must declare mappedBy pointing to the parent field. Use CascadeType.ALL to propagate lifecycle events and orphanRemoval = true to delete children removed from the parent list. Always write defensive helper methods on the parent entity (addChild/removeChild) to set both sides of the relationship in memory, preventing inconsistent persistence states.
follow_up_questions: What happens if you omit mappedBy on a @OneToMany relationship?
Why should you avoid using @ManyToMany with CascadeType.REMOVE?

questions.question_title: How does Hibernate Dirty Checking work, and when is the Session flushed?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how Hibernate tracks entity changes between snapshot copies. What triggers a session flush (commit, query execution, explicit flush), and what is the difference between flush() and commit()?
expected_answer_points: Snapshot creation: When an entity is loaded into the Persistence Context, Hibernate creates a deep-copy snapshot of its state.
Dirty checking: During flush, Hibernate compares the current state of managed entities against their snapshot. If different, it generates an UPDATE SQL statement.
Flush triggers: 1) Transaction commit; 2) Before executing a JPQL/native query that accesses the table (FlushModeType.AUTO); 3) Explicit em.flush().
Flush vs Commit: flush() synchronizes in-memory SQL statements to the database transaction log, but does NOT commit. commit() flushes and makes changes permanent and visible to other transactions.
questions.sample_answer: When an entity becomes managed, Hibernate saves a snapshot of its fields. At flush time, it compares each managed entity against its snapshot. If fields changed, Hibernate automatically issues SQL UPDATE statements without needing repository.save(). Flushing synchronizes SQL to the database connection buffer and occurs before queries (FlushModeType.AUTO) or at transaction commit. Unlike commit(), a flush can still be rolled back.
follow_up_questions: How does bytecode enhancement optimize dirty checking in large entities?
Why does executing a native SQL query trigger a flush of all pending entity changes?

questions.subtopic: JPQL vs Criteria API vs Native Queries
questions.question_title: Compare JPQL, Spring Data Specifications (Criteria API), and Native SQL queries.
questions.question_prompt: When should you use JPQL vs Criteria API / Specifications vs Native SQL? Discuss portability, type safety, dynamic filtering, and database-specific feature utilization.
expected_answer_points: JPQL (Java Persistence Query Language): Operates on entity objects and relationships rather than database tables. Portable across databases. Checked at application startup.
Criteria API / Specifications: Programmatic, type-safe query construction. Best for dynamic search filters (e.g. e-commerce search with optional price, category, rating).
Native SQL: Raw SQL executed directly on DB (@Query(value = '...', nativeQuery = true)). Best for database-specific optimizations, window functions, CTEs, or bulk updates.
Native query drawback: Couples application to a specific database engine and does not support automatic pagination counting in complex joins without countQuery.
questions.sample_answer: JPQL queries entity objects rather than tables, making queries database-agnostic. Spring Data Specifications (built on Criteria API) provide type-safe dynamic query building, ideal for multi-criteria search forms with optional filters. Native SQL is reserved for database-specific features like recursive CTEs, window functions, or specialized performance indexing, but sacrifices database portability and entity lifecycle management.
follow_up_questions: Why must you specify a separate countQuery in Spring Data when using native queries with Pageable?
What is the difference between Class-based DTO projections and Interface-based projections in Spring Data JPA?

questions.question_title: Explain First-Level Cache and Second-Level Cache in Hibernate.
questions.question_prompt: Compare Session-scoped First-Level Cache and SessionFactory-scoped Second-Level Cache (Ehcache, Redis, Hazelcast). How does query caching work, and what are cache invalidation risks?
expected_answer_points: First-Level Cache: Bound to the active Session/EntityManager. Mandatory and cannot be disabled. Guarantees that multiple find() calls for the same ID in one transaction return the same Java reference.
Second-Level Cache (L2C): Bound to SessionFactory / ApplicationContext. Shared across all sessions and transactions. Pluggable (Ehcache, Infinispan, Redis).
Entity caching vs Query caching: L2C stores entity state dehydrated as arrays. Query cache stores query parameter keys and resulting entity ID lists.
Invalidation: Frequent updates to a cached table invalidate the query cache, causing performance degradation.
Best for: Static or read-mostly master data (e.g. countries, product categories, tax rates).
questions.sample_answer: The First-Level Cache is session-scoped, mandatory, and caches managed entities within a single transaction. The Second-Level Cache is shared across all sessions and survives transactions, using distributed providers like Redis or Ehcache. It caches read-heavy, rarely-changing reference data (like country codes). Query caching stores lists of entity IDs matching specific query parameters, but must be used cautiously because any write to the underlying table invalidates cached query results.
follow_up_questions: What are the concurrency strategies available for Hibernate Second-Level Cache (read-only, read-write, nonstrict-read-write, transactional)?
Why is caching volatile write-heavy entities in L2C an anti-pattern?

questions.subtopic: equals and hashCode in JPA Entities
questions.question_title: How should equals() and hashCode() be implemented on JPA Entities?
questions.question_prompt: Why is using database generated ID (@GeneratedValue) or IDE default field generation inside equals/hashCode dangerous for JPA entities? What is the recommended business key approach?
expected_answer_points: Problem with @Id: Before persist(), the ID is null. If an entity is added to a HashSet while transient (hashCode calculated from null ID), and then persisted, its ID changes. hashSet.contains(entity) will return false!
Problem with getter/field access: Hibernate proxies return null when accessing private fields directly; getters must be used (getId() instead of this.id).
Problem with getClass(): Hibernate proxies use subclasses (Entity$HibernateProxy$xyz). equals() must check 'other instanceof MyEntity' rather than getClass() == other.getClass().

Best practice: Use a unique natural business key (e.g. UUID, email, ISBN) if available. If none exists, return a constant hashCode (e.g. return getClass().hashCode()) and compare IDs in equals() only if both are non-null.
questions.sample_answer: Using a generated @Id in equals/hashCode is dangerous because before persisting, the ID is null. If inserted into a HashSet while transient, its hash code changes upon persistence, corrupting the Set. Furthermore, comparing fields directly fails on Hibernate proxies because uninitialized proxy fields are null (getters must be used), and checking getClass() fails against proxy subclasses. The best approach is using a natural business key (like UUID), or using instanceof with getter comparisons.
follow_up_questions: Why does returning a constant hashCode (e.g. return 31) for an entity satisfy the hash contract while avoiding ID mutation bugs?
Why should collections (e.g. items in Order) never be included in an entity's equals() or hashCode()?

questions.question_title: Compare JPA Inheritance Strategies: SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED, and TABLE_PER_CLASS.
questions.question_prompt: Explain the trade-offs of SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED, and TABLE_PER_CLASS. Which provides the best query performance, which enforces NOT NULL constraints, and which uses a discriminator column (@DiscriminatorColumn)?
expected_answer_points: SINGLE_TABLE (default): All classes in hierarchy mapped to 1 table with a @DiscriminatorColumn. Fastest queries (no joins required), but subclass columns must be nullable (cannot enforce NOT NULL at DB level).

JOINED: Base class and each subclass have their own tables; subclass table holds only specific fields + foreign key to base table. Enforces NOT NULL constraints and normalization, but polymorphic queries require expensive multi-table SQL JOINs.

TABLE_PER_CLASS: Each concrete subclass has its own independent table containing all base and subclass fields. Eliminates joins for single subclass queries, but polymorphic queries (SELECT from Base) require slow SQL UNIONs.
questions.sample_answer: SINGLE_TABLE maps the entire inheritance hierarchy to a single table with a discriminator column. It gives the fastest polymorphic queries (zero joins) but cannot enforce database-level NOT NULL constraints on subclass columns. JOINED normalizes data into separate tables linked by foreign keys, supporting NOT NULL constraints, but requires SQL JOINs on polymorphic queries. TABLE_PER_CLASS duplicates base columns into separate tables per subclass, requiring expensive SQL UNIONs for polymorphic queries.
follow_up_questions: What is @MappedSuperclass and how does it differ from JPA entity inheritance?
When is @DiscriminatorValue needed in SINGLE_TABLE and JOINED inheritance?

questions.question_title: How do bulk updates with @Modifying affect the JPA Persistence Context?
questions.question_prompt: Why must @Modifying accompany UPDATE/DELETE JPQL queries? What happens to entities already in the First-Level Cache when a bulk update runs, and why is clearAutomatically = true needed?
expected_answer_points: @Modifying instructs Spring Data that the @Query is a DML write statement (executeNonQuery) rather than a SELECT.
Bypasses Persistence Context: Bulk UPDATE/DELETE queries translate directly into SQL executed on the database, completely bypassing Hibernate's First-Level Cache and dirty checking.
Stale Data Risk: Entities already loaded into the current EntityManager retain their pre-update values in memory.
clearAutomatically = true: Automatically clears the persistence context (em.clear()) after executing the bulk query, ensuring subsequent queries reload fresh state from the DB.
flushAutomatically = true: Flushes any pending entity modifications before executing the bulk query.
questions.sample_answer: @Modifying tells Spring Data that a JPQL query is an UPDATE or DELETE statement. Because bulk queries execute directly against the database, they bypass the Persistence Context. If entities were already loaded in memory, they become stale. Setting @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true) forces Hibernate to clear the first-level cache immediately after the update so subsequent operations fetch updated values from the database.
follow_up_questions: What happens if you omit @Modifying on an @Query with an UPDATE statement?
Why don't bulk updates trigger entity lifecycle callbacks (@PreUpdate, @PostUpdate)?

questions.question_title: How do you handle Distributed Transactions in Microservices using the Saga Pattern?
questions.question_prompt: Why is Two-Phase Commit (2PC) unsuitable for distributed microservices? Compare Choreography-based Sagas and Orchestration-based Sagas, and explain how compensating transactions handle failures.
expected_answer_points: Why not 2PC: Two-Phase Commit is blocking, creates tight coupling, and suffers from single coordinator failure and poor latency across network boundaries (violates CAP availability).
Saga Pattern: A sequence of local database transactions where each service updates its own database and publishes an event/message triggering the next step.
Compensating Transactions: If a step fails, the saga executes backward compensating transactions to undo preceding changes (eventual consistency).
Choreography: Services listen to domain events and decide when to act (decentralized, good for simple flows; hard to trace as complexity grows).
Orchestration: A central Saga Orchestrator tells participants what local transactions to execute (centralized, easy to monitor, handles complex state machines).
questions.sample_answer: Two-Phase Commit is a blocking coordinator protocol that reduces availability and throughput across distributed systems. The Saga pattern breaks distributed transactions into a sequence of local ACID transactions. If a step fails (e.g. payment rejected), the Saga triggers compensating transactions in reverse order to semantically undo earlier actions (e.g. un-reserving inventory). In Choreography, services react to Kafka events independently; in Orchestration, a dedicated coordinator (like Temporal or Camunda) manages the state machine.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between a compensating transaction and a database rollback?
How do you handle a failure inside a compensating transaction itself?

questions.question_title: How does the Circuit Breaker Pattern work with Resilience4j?
questions.question_prompt: Explain the three states of a Circuit Breaker: CLOSED, OPEN, and HALF-OPEN. How do sliding window metrics, failure rate thresholds, wait duration in open state, and fallback mechanisms prevent cascading failures?
expected_answer_points: Problem: A slow or failing downstream service causes thread exhaustion across calling services, leading to cascading failures throughout the system.
CLOSED state: Normal operation; requests pass through. Tracks failure rate in a sliding window (count-based or time-based).
OPEN state: When failure rate exceeds threshold (e.g. > 50%), the circuit trips OPEN. All calls immediately fail-fast or execute fallbacks without calling the downstream service.

HALF-OPEN state: After waitDurationInOpenState expires, circuit enters HALF-OPEN. It permits a limited number of trial calls; if they succeed, it returns to CLOSED; if any fail, it trips back to OPEN.
Fallback method: Returns cached data, default values, or queues the action for background retry.
questions.sample_answer: A circuit breaker prevents cascading failures by stopping calls to failing downstream services. In CLOSED state, requests flow normally while monitoring failure rates. If failures exceed the threshold (e.g. 50%), the circuit flips to OPEN, immediately short-circuiting calls to fallback methods and saving threads. After a configured wait duration, it enters HALF-OPEN to send probe requests: if healthy, it resets to CLOSED; if failures persist, it re-opens.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between a count-based sliding window and a time-based sliding window in Resilience4j?
Why must fallback methods have the exact same method signature plus an additional Throwable parameter?

questions.question_title: What are the core responsibilities of an API Gateway (Spring Cloud Gateway)?
questions.question_prompt: Explain the role of an API Gateway in microservices architectures: Routing, SSL termination, Authentication/Authorization, Rate Limiting (Token Bucket with Redis), Request/Response transformation, and Cross-Cutting Metrics.
expected_answer_points: Single entry point for all external clients, insulating internal service topologies.
Routing & Load Balancing: Dynamically routes incoming requests to downstream microservice instances.
Authentication & Token Validation: Centralizes JWT verification at the edge so internal services can trust authenticated claims.
Rate Limiting: Uses Redis-backed Token Bucket algorithm (RequestRateLimiter) to protect backends from DDoS and abuse.
Cross-cutting concerns: SSL termination, CORS handling, unified access logging, and tracing header injection.
Spring Cloud Gateway uses reactive Netty and non-blocking filters (GatewayFilter, GlobalFilter).
questions.sample_answer: An API Gateway acts as the single reverse-proxy entry point for client applications. It centralizes edge concerns: validating authentication tokens (JWT), routing requests to internal services, terminating SSL, enforcing rate limits via Redis token-bucket filters, and providing observability. By handling cross-cutting concerns at the gateway, downstream microservices can focus purely on domain business logic without duplicating boilerplate security and CORS checks.
follow_up_questions: Why did Spring Cloud Gateway replace Netflix Zuul 1.x (blocking I/O vs non-blocking Netty)?
What is the 'Backends for Frontends' (BFF) pattern?

questions.subtopic: Service Discovery: Eureka vs Kubernetes DNS
questions.question_title: Compare Eureka Service Discovery with Kubernetes Native DNS Discovery.
questions.question_prompt: Explain how client-side load balancing with Eureka and Spring Cloud LoadBalancer works. Why are teams moving away from Eureka in favor of Kubernetes Services and CoreDNS?
expected_answer_points: Eureka: Application-level registry. Microservices register host/port with Eureka server via periodic heartbeats. Clients fetch the registry and use Spring Cloud LoadBalancer to select an instance.

Kubernetes DNS: Platform-level discovery. Every Kubernetes Service receives a stable DNS name (e.g. order-service.default.svc.cluster.local) and ClusterIP. Kube-proxy / iptables handle load balancing to healthy pods.
Why K8s is preferred: Language-agnostic, built into the container orchestrator, eliminates maintaining dedicated Eureka server clusters, and handles liveness/readiness probes natively.
questions.sample_answer: Eureka is an application-level service registry where microservices self-register and clients query Eureka to perform client-side load balancing. In containerized environments, Kubernetes native DNS replaces Eureka: Kubernetes assigns a stable internal DNS name and virtual IP to each Service, and kube-proxy handles load balancing transparently to healthy pods. This eliminates managing separate Eureka infrastructure and works across any programming language.
follow_up_questions: What is Eureka Self-Preservation Mode and when does it trigger?
How does client-side load balancing compare with server-side load balancing?

questions.question_title: How does the Transactional Outbox Pattern solve dual-write data inconsistencies?
questions.question_prompt: What is the dual-write problem when updating a database and publishing an event to Kafka in the same HTTP request? How does the Transactional Outbox pattern with Debezium (CDC) solve it?
expected_answer_points: Dual-write problem: If a service saves an entity to SQL DB and publishes to Kafka, one can succeed while the other fails (e.g. DB commits but Kafka network drops, or Kafka succeeds but DB transaction rolls back).
Transactional Outbox solution: Write the business entity AND an outbox message record into the SAME relational database within a SINGLE local ACID transaction.
Message relay: A separate process reads the outbox table and publishes events to Kafka.

Debezium / CDC (Change Data Capture): Tails the database transaction log (Postgres WAL or MySQL binlog) and publishes outbox rows to Kafka with zero polling overhead and exactly-once delivery guarantees at DB level.
questions.sample_answer: The dual-write problem occurs when updating a database and publishing to a message broker in the same action: network failures can cause the DB to commit while Kafka fails (or vice versa), leading to data inconsistency. The Transactional Outbox pattern solves this by writing the event into an 'outbox' table in the same local ACID transaction as the business entity. A Change Data Capture (CDC) tool like Debezium streams outbox table changes from the database commit log directly into Kafka reliably.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between polling publisher and transaction log tailing for the Outbox pattern?
How do downstream consumers guarantee idempotent processing of outbox events?

questions.question_title: Compare Synchronous REST/gRPC vs Asynchronous Event-Driven Communication in Microservices.
questions.question_prompt: When should microservices communicate synchronously via REST/OpenFeign or gRPC versus asynchronously via message brokers (Kafka/RabbitMQ)? Discuss coupling, latency, availability, and failure isolation.
expected_answer_points: Synchronous (REST/gRPC): Immediate response needed (e.g. querying current user profile or checking live fraud risk). Drawbacks: temporal coupling, cascading latency, decreased system availability (availability = A_1 * A_2 * A_3).
gRPC advantages over REST: Protocol Buffers binary serialization (smaller payloads, faster parsing), HTTP/2 multiplexing, strongly-typed contract.

Asynchronous (Kafka/RabbitMQ): Fire-and-forget or event notification (e.g. OrderCreated, SendNotification). Benefits: temporal decoupling, producer does not block on consumer availability, natural load leveling/buffering.
Best practice: Use synchronous for immediate read queries; use asynchronous event-driven for mutations and cross-service state propagation.
questions.sample_answer: Synchronous communication (REST, gRPC) is suitable when the caller requires immediate data to proceed. However, it creates temporal coupling and reduces availability because failure in any downstream service immediately impacts the caller. Asynchronous event-driven communication (Kafka, RabbitMQ) decouples services: producers publish events and continue immediately without waiting for consumers, providing resilience against downstream outages and smoothing traffic spikes.
follow_up_questions: How does HTTP/2 multiplexing in gRPC overcome HTTP/1.1 head-of-line blocking?
What is the Request-Reply pattern over asynchronous message brokers?

questions.question_title: Explain the CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) pattern.
questions.question_prompt: Why separate write models (Commands) from read models (Queries) in microservices? How are read models kept up to date using event sourcing or domain events, and what is eventual consistency lag?
expected_answer_points: CQRS separates data mutation operations (Commands) from data retrieval operations (Queries) into distinct models.
Problem solved: Relational schemas optimized for normalized transactional writes (3NF) perform poorly for complex multi-table joins and reporting queries.

Architecture: Write model updates the write DB (e.g. PostgreSQL). Domain events are published to Kafka. Event consumers update read-optimized materialized views (e.g. Elasticsearch for full-text search, Redis for caching, MongoDB for denormalized documents).
Trade-off: Eventual consistency — there is a brief replication lag between command acceptance and read model update.
questions.sample_answer: CQRS separates the write model (commands) from the read model (queries). Writing uses a normalized relational database optimized for ACID compliance and validation, while reading uses denormalized read stores (such as Elasticsearch or MongoDB) optimized for fast queries. When a write completes, an event is emitted to update the read models asynchronously. The system accepts eventual consistency in exchange for massive read scalability and query flexibility.
follow_up_questions: How do user interfaces handle eventual consistency lag when a user creates a record and is immediately redirected to a list view?
How does Event Sourcing complement CQRS?

questions.question_title: How is configuration externalized and dynamically refreshed in microservices?
questions.question_prompt: Explain the 12-Factor App principle for configuration. Compare Spring Cloud Config Server with Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets. How does @RefreshScope enable dynamic property updates without restarting services?
expected_answer_points: 12-Factor App rule: Strict separation of config from code; store config in environment or external store.
Spring Cloud Config: Central Git-backed configuration server providing versioned property files over HTTP.
@RefreshScope: Spring Cloud annotation that recreates beans when /actuator/refresh is called or Spring Cloud Bus emits a refresh event, reloading property values without restarting JVM.

Kubernetes approach: ConfigMaps (non-sensitive properties) and Secrets (base64-encoded/vault-mounted credentials) mounted as environment variables or filesystem volumes. Standard in modern cloud deployments.
questions.sample_answer: Externalized configuration separates code from environment settings (12-Factor App). Spring Cloud Config centralizes configuration in a Git repository and serves properties over HTTP. Beans annotated with @RefreshScope can be re-instantiated at runtime when an actuator refresh event occurs. In modern cloud-native architectures, Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets are preferred, mounting configuration as environment variables or volume files directly into pods.
follow_up_questions: What are the security risks of mounting sensitive credentials via plain environment variables in Kubernetes?
How does HashiCorp Vault integrate with Spring Cloud Vault for dynamic secret rotation?

questions.question_title: Explain the Bulkhead and Rate Limiter resilience patterns in Resilience4j.
questions.question_prompt: How does the Bulkhead pattern (Semaphore vs ThreadPool) prevent one failing component from consuming all server resources? How does the Token Bucket rate limiter protect services from overload?
expected_answer_points: Bulkhead origin: Watertight compartments in ships that prevent the entire vessel from sinking if one section breaches.
ThreadPool Bulkhead: Isolates operations into dedicated thread pools with bounded queues. If service A becomes slow, only its thread pool exhausts, leaving threads available for service B.
Semaphore Bulkhead: Limits the number of concurrent executions using a semaphore without creating separate thread pools (low overhead).
Rate Limiter: Limits request invocations per time window (e.g. 100 requests per second) to prevent resource starvation or comply with external API quotas.
questions.sample_answer: The Bulkhead pattern partitions system resources so that failures in one component cannot exhaust the entire application. Resilience4j offers ThreadPool bulkheads (isolating tasks into separate thread pools with bounded queues) and Semaphore bulkheads (capping concurrent executions on the current thread). The Rate Limiter restricts the number of calls per time period, protecting downstream dependencies from sudden traffic spikes.
follow_up_questions: When would you choose a Semaphore Bulkhead over a ThreadPool Bulkhead?
How does Resilience4j TimeLimiter differ from standard connection timeouts?

questions.question_title: How do you decompose a Monolith into Microservices using Domain-Driven Design (DDD)?
questions.question_prompt: Explain Bounded Contexts, Ubiquitous Language, Aggregate Roots, and the Strangler Fig pattern for migrating legacy monoliths to microservices.
expected_answer_points: Bounded Context: Explicit boundary within which a domain model applies. The term 'Account' may mean a billing profile in the Billing context, but user login credentials in the Identity context.
Aggregate Root: Cluster of domain objects treated as a single unit for data changes (e.g. Order and OrderItems). External objects only hold references to the Aggregate Root.
Database per Service: Each microservice must own its private database; direct cross-database queries are forbidden.
Strangler Fig pattern: Incrementally replace pieces of the monolith by placing an API Gateway in front and routing new or migrated endpoints to microservices until the monolith is retired.
questions.sample_answer: Domain-Driven Design identifies microservice boundaries by finding Bounded Contexts, where terms have specific business meanings (e.g. Customer in Sales vs Support). Each microservice owns its domain aggregates and private database. Rather than a risky rewrite, teams use the Strangler Fig pattern: placing an API Gateway in front of the monolith and intercepting specific functionality (e.g. Notification or Order Service) into new microservices incrementally until the monolith is shrunk.
follow_up_questions: What is the anti-pattern known as a 'Distributed Monolith'?
Why must microservices never share a common relational database schema?

questions.question_title: How does Spring Cloud OpenFeign simplify HTTP inter-service communication?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how Spring Cloud OpenFeign creates declarative REST clients from Java interfaces. How do you configure timeouts, custom ErrorDecoder, RequestInterceptor (for JWT forwarding), and Fallbacks?
expected_answer_points: Declarative: Define a Java interface with Spring MVC annotations (@GetMapping, @PathVariable) and annotate with @FeignClient(name = 'payment-service'). Spring generates the dynamic proxy implementation.
Timeouts: Configure connectTimeout and readTimeout per client in application.yml.
RequestInterceptor: Intercepts outgoing requests to copy authentication headers (e.g. Bearer token from incoming request) into the downstream Feign call.
ErrorDecoder: Maps HTTP 4xx/5xx responses from the downstream service into specific Java domain exceptions instead of generic FeignException.
Resilience: Integrates with Resilience4j for circuit breakers and fallback factory implementations.
questions.sample_answer: Spring Cloud OpenFeign allows writing declarative HTTP clients: you define an interface with Spring MVC annotations, and Feign generates the proxy implementation at runtime. Use RequestInterceptor to copy authorization tokens from the current SecurityContext into outgoing Feign requests. Custom ErrorDecoder implementations translate downstream HTTP errors into application exceptions. Pairing Feign with Resilience4j provides circuit breakers and fallback handling.
follow_up_questions: Why must you use a FallbackFactory instead of a simple fallback class if you need access to the root cause exception?
What HTTP client does Feign use by default, and why should it be replaced with Apache HttpClient or OkHttp?

questions.question_title: Explain the internal architecture of Apache Kafka: Brokers, Topics, Partitions, and Offsets.
questions.question_prompt: How does Kafka organize data? Explain how partitions provide horizontal scalability, how record keys determine partition assignment, and how sequential append-only logs enable high write throughput.
expected_answer_points: Topic: Logical stream of records. Split into one or more Partitions.
Partition: An ordered, immutable commit log of records. Unit of parallelism and horizontal scale in Kafka.
Offset: Unique, monotonically increasing integer assigned to each message within a partition.
Key partitioning: Records with the same non-null key are hashed (murmur2) and guaranteed to land on the exact same partition, preserving strict ordering.
High throughput: Kafka writes to disk sequentially (O(1) append), relies on OS page cache, and uses the zero-copy sendfile system call to transmit bytes directly from page cache to network socket.
questions.sample_answer: Kafka organizes data into Topics, which are split across multiple Partitions for parallel processing. A partition is an immutable append-only commit log on disk where each record receives a sequential Offset. If a message has a key, Kafka hashes it to assign it to a specific partition, guaranteeing strict per-key ordering. Kafka achieves high throughput by leveraging sequential disk I/O, heavy use of OS page cache, and zero-copy network transfer.
follow_up_questions: What happens to message ordering if a topic has multiple partitions and messages have null keys?
Can Kafka partition count be decreased on an existing topic?

questions.question_title: How do Consumer Groups work, and what triggers a Consumer Rebalance?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how partitions are assigned across consumers in a consumer group. What happens when consumer count > partition count? What causes consumer rebalances, and how do Cooperative Sticky Assignors reduce rebalance stop-the-world pauses?
expected_answer_points: Consumer Group: A group of consumers cooperating to consume a topic. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer within the group at any time.
Sizing rule: If consumers > partitions, surplus consumers sit idle with 0 partitions assigned.

Rebalance triggers: 1) Consumer joins or leaves (clean shutdown or crash); 2) Consumer heartbeat failure (max.poll.interval.ms exceeded or heartbeat.interval.ms timeout); 3) New partitions added to topic.
Eager rebalancing: All consumers revoke all partitions and stop consuming until reassignment finishes (stop-the-world).
