questions.sample_answer: Two-Phase Locking guarantees conflict serializability by dividing locking into a Growing Phase (acquiring locks without releasing) and a Shrinking Phase (releasing locks without acquiring new ones). Basic 2PL can cause cascading aborts if a transaction releases a lock early and rolls back. Strict 2PL (used in production databases) mandates holding all Exclusive locks until final commit or rollback, completely eliminating cascading rollbacks.
follow_up_questions: Does Strict 2PL prevent deadlocks?
What is Lock Escalation in relational database management systems?

questions.question_title: Explain the on-disk storage difference between Clustered and Secondary Indexes.
questions.question_prompt: How does the presence of a clustered index impact table insertion and fragmentation? Why does updating an indexed column require updating both the clustered and secondary indexes?
expected_answer_points: Clustered index leaf pages contain the actual data rows; the table IS the clustered index.
Insertion impact: New rows must be inserted into the specific leaf page matching their sorted key. Random key inserts (e.g. UUIDv4) cause Page Splits, fragmentation, and high disk I/O.
Secondary index structure: Leaf nodes store the index key and the clustered key (or RID).
Update impact: Updating a non-indexed column requires only updating the data page. Updating an indexed column requires deleting and re-inserting the secondary B-Tree node, plus page reorganization.
Secondary index double lookup: Lookup traverses secondary index to find PK, then traverses clustered index to read table row.
questions.sample_answer: In a clustered index, the leaf nodes ARE the actual physical table rows sorted by the key. Random key insertions cause page splitting when full pages must split to insert rows in sorted order, creating fragmentation. Secondary indexes store the secondary key and the clustered primary key. Updating an indexed column forces the engine to delete and re-insert nodes in the secondary index tree, which is why columns subject to frequent updates make poor index candidates.
follow_up_questions: What is an Index Page Split and how does it affect write throughput?
What is Fill Factor and how does configuring it reduce page splits?

questions.question_title: Compare LSM Trees (Log-Structured Merge-Trees) and B-Trees for database storage.
questions.question_prompt: Why do write-heavy databases (Cassandra, RocksDB) use LSM Trees instead of B-Trees? Explain MemTable (RAM), Commit Log (WAL), SSTables (immutable disk files), and Compaction.
expected_answer_points: B-Tree write penalty: In-place page updates require random I/O writes across disk, causing I/O bottlenecks under high write throughput.
LSM Tree write optimization: Writes are appended sequentially to a WAL on disk and buffered in an in-memory sorted structure (MemTable e.g. SkipList). Ultra-fast O(1) writes.
Flushing: When MemTable fills, it flushes to disk as an immutable, sorted SSTable (Sorted String Table). Zero random writes.
Compaction: Background threads merge multiple overlapping SSTables into new sorted files (removing deleted tombstone records).
Trade-off: LSM trades read performance and compaction CPU/disk overhead for massive write throughput.
questions.sample_answer: B-Trees perform random in-place updates on disk pages, creating I/O bottlenecks under heavy writes. LSM Trees optimize writes by appending sequentially to a commit log and buffering into an in-memory MemTable. When full, MemTables flush to disk as immutable, sorted SSTables. Writes are strictly sequential, delivering incredible write throughput. To handle reads across multiple files, background compaction merges SSTables, trading read latency and compaction I/O for write speed.
follow_up_questions: How do Bloom Filters speed up read lookups in LSM Tree storage engines?
What is Write Amplification in LSM Trees?

questions.question_title: How does the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol achieve atomicity across distributed databases?
questions.question_prompt: Explain Prepare Phase (voting) and Commit Phase in 2PC. What happens if the Coordinator crashes, and why does 2PC block resources during network partitions?
expected_answer_points: 2PC achieves atomic commits across multiple autonomous database nodes managed by a Coordinator.
Phase 1 (Prepare): Coordinator sends PREPARE message to all cohorts. Cohorts execute transaction locally, write undo/redo logs, acquire locks, and vote YES (ready to commit) or NO.
Phase 2 (Commit/Abort): If ALL cohorts vote YES, coordinator logs COMMIT to its disk and sends GLOBAL_COMMIT to cohorts. If any cohort votes NO or times out, coordinator sends GLOBAL_ABORT.
Flaw (Blocking Protocol): If the Coordinator crashes after cohorts vote YES but before sending GLOBAL_COMMIT, cohorts are left in doubt holding database locks indefinitely, blocking other traffic.
Violates CAP theorem availability.
questions.sample_answer: Two-Phase Commit coordinates atomic transactions across distributed databases. In Phase 1 (Prepare), the coordinator asks all nodes to prepare: nodes write undo/redo logs, acquire locks, and vote YES or NO. In Phase 2, if all voted YES, the coordinator broadcasts GLOBAL_COMMIT; otherwise it broadcasts GLOBAL_ABORT. The fatal flaw of 2PC is that it is a blocking protocol: if the coordinator crashes during Phase 2, cohorts must hold locks indefinitely, blocking the system.
follow_up_questions: What is Three-Phase Commit (3PC) and why is it rarely used in practice?
Why has the Saga Pattern largely replaced 2PC in microservices architectures?

questions.question_title: When should you use Bitmap Indexes and Inverted Indexes instead of B-Trees?
questions.question_prompt: Compare Bitmap Indexes (low cardinality) and Inverted Indexes (full-text search / search engines). Why are Bitmap indexes ideal for OLAP data warehousing but terrible for OLTP write-heavy databases?
expected_answer_points: Bitmap Index: Creates a bit array (0s and 1s) for each distinct value in a column. E.g. gender: Male [1, 0, 1], Female [0, 1, 0].
OLAP superpower: Complex multi-column boolean queries (WHERE gender = 'M' AND marital_status = 'S' AND state = 'CA') evaluate using ultra-fast hardware bitwise operations (AND, OR, NOT).
OLTP disaster: Modifying a single row locks the ENTIRE bitmap segment, paralyzing concurrent writes.
Inverted Index: Maps words/tokens to the list of document/row IDs containing them (used by Elasticsearch, Lucene, and PostgreSQL GIN).
questions.sample_answer: Bitmap indexes create a bit vector for each unique column value, making them exceptionally fast for OLAP data warehouses where queries combine low-cardinality filters using CPU bitwise operators (AND, OR). However, they are unusable in OLTP write-heavy systems because modifying a row requires locking the entire bitmap vector. Inverted indexes map tokens to matching document IDs, serving as the foundation for full-text search engines like Elasticsearch.
follow_up_questions: What is Roaring Bitmap compression?
How does a PostgreSQL GIN index utilize inverted index concepts for array and JSONB queries?

questions.question_title: Compare Horizontal Sharding, Vertical Partitioning, and Directory-Based Sharding.
questions.question_prompt: Explain how databases scale horizontally past single-node limits. Compare Range-Based Sharding, Hash-Based Sharding, and Directory-Based Sharding. What are the challenges of cross-shard joins and distributed transactions?
expected_answer_points: Vertical Partitioning: Splitting columns into separate tables/databases (e.g. separating user profile from user billing).
Horizontal Sharding: Partitioning rows across multiple database servers based on a Shard Key.
Range-Based Sharding: Sharding by key ranges (A-F on Shard 1, G-M on Shard 2). Easy range queries, but creates write hotspots on popular ranges.
Hash-Based Sharding: Hash(shard_key) % num_shards. Uniform write distribution, but range queries become scatter-gather operations across all shards.
Challenges: Cross-shard joins are impossible or slow; cross-shard transactions require distributed 2PC; re-sharding requires migrating gigabytes of data (solved via Consistent Hashing).
questions.sample_answer: Horizontal sharding splits rows across multiple database nodes using a shard key. Range-based sharding divides by value ranges, simplifying range scans but creating hotspots on active ranges. Hash-based sharding applies a hash function (hash(id) % N) to distribute writes evenly, but forces range queries to execute scatter-gather scans across all nodes. The architectural challenges of sharding include loss of relational integrity, expensive cross-shard joins, and complex distributed re-balancing.
follow_up_questions: How does Consistent Hashing minimize data movement when adding or removing database shards?
What is a Scatter-Gather query pattern in sharded systems?

questions.question_title: Explain the fundamental differences between a Process and a Thread.
questions.question_prompt: Compare Processes and Threads in terms of memory address space, PCB (Process Control Block) vs TCB (Thread Control Block), context switching overhead, and IPC vs shared memory.
expected_answer_points: Process: Independent program in execution with its own isolated virtual address space (Code, Data, Heap, Stack), file descriptors, and PCB.
Thread: Lightweight unit of execution within a process. Threads of the same process SHARE the Code, Data, Heap, and file descriptors, but maintain PRIVATE Stacks, Registers, and PC (Program Counter).
Context Switch Overhead: Process context switch is heavy (invalidates CPU MMU TLB cache, switches page tables). Thread context switch is lightweight (keeps same page directory, retains TLB cache).
Communication: Processes require IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory); threads communicate directly via shared heap memory (requiring synchronization primitives to avoid race conditions).
questions.sample_answer: A process is an isolated execution environment with its own private virtual address space and file descriptors. A thread is a lightweight execution unit inside a process; threads within the same process share the heap, global variables, and code, but keep private execution stacks and program counters. Process context switching is expensive because it swaps page tables and flushes the CPU TLB cache, whereas thread switching preserves the memory context, making it substantially faster.
follow_up_questions: What is the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) and why does a process context switch invalidate it?
What is a zombie process vs an orphan process in Linux?

questions.question_title: Explain the 4 Coffman Conditions for Deadlocks and how to prevent them.
questions.question_prompt: Detail Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. How does eliminating any ONE condition guarantee deadlock prevention? What is Dijkstra's Banker's Algorithm?
expected_answer_points: Four mandatory Coffman Conditions: 1) Mutual Exclusion: Resource can be held by only one process at a time; 2) Hold and Wait: Process holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire others; 3) No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly taken from a process until released; 4) Circular Wait: Closed chain of processes where each waits for a resource held by the next.
Deadlock Prevention breaks at least one condition: Break Circular Wait by enforcing a strict global numerical acquisition order for all locks; Break Hold and Wait by requesting all resources upfront.
Banker's Algorithm: Deadlock avoidance algorithm that tests for safety by simulating allocation of predetermined maximum resources to prevent entering an unsafe state.
questions.sample_answer: Deadlocks require four simultaneous Coffman conditions: Mutual Exclusion (non-shareable resources), Hold and Wait (holding resources while requesting more), No Preemption (resources cannot be confiscated), and Circular Wait (a circular dependency of threads waiting on each other). Breaking any one condition prevents deadlocks. In software engineering, the most practical defense is breaking Circular Wait by enforcing a strict global lock hierarchy (always acquiring Lock A before Lock B across the entire codebase).
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between Deadlock Prevention and Deadlock Avoidance?
What is Livelock and how does it differ from Deadlock?

questions.subtopic: Virtual Memory, Paging, and Page Faults
questions.question_title: How does Virtual Memory work with Paging and Page Faults?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how the Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates virtual addresses to physical addresses using Page Tables. What happens during a Page Fault, and what is Thrashing?
expected_answer_points: Virtual Memory: Provides each process with the illusion of a contiguous, private memory space larger than physical RAM.
Paging: Virtual address space split into fixed-size Pages (typically 4KB); physical RAM split into matching Page Frames.
MMU translation: Uses multi-level Page Tables and TLB (hardware cache) to map Virtual Page Numbers to Physical Frame Numbers.

Page Fault: Triggered when a process accesses a page marked invalid/not present in RAM. The OS trap suspends the process, fetches the page from swap disk into a free RAM frame, updates the page table present bit, and resumes instruction.
Thrashing: Occurs when system RAM is exhausted and the OS spends more time swapping pages to/from disk than executing actual instructions (CPU utilization plummets).
questions.sample_answer: Virtual memory maps a process's virtual addresses to physical RAM frames through page tables managed by the MMU. When a process accesses a memory address whose page is not in physical RAM, the MMU triggers a Page Fault interrupt. The OS pauses the process, reads the missing page from swap disk into an available RAM frame, updates the page table, and resumes execution. Thrashing occurs when high memory pressure causes continuous page faults, starving the CPU with disk I/O.
follow_up_questions: Compare page replacement algorithms: LRU, FIFO, and Clock (Second Chance).
What are HugePages (2MB/1GB) in Linux and why do databases (PostgreSQL/Oracle) use them?

questions.question_title: Compare Mutex, Counting Semaphore, and Spinlock synchronization primitives.
questions.question_prompt: When should you use a Mutex versus a Semaphore versus a Spinlock? Explain ownership (locking/unlocking thread constraints), busy-waiting vs sleeping, and Priority Inversion.
expected_answer_points: Mutex (Mutual Exclusion): Binary locking mechanism with OWNERSHIP. Only the thread that locked the mutex is allowed to unlock it. Put threads to sleep if unavailable.

Semaphore: Signaling mechanism with a counter. Has NO ownership (Thread A can wait/decrement, Thread B can post/increment). Used for resource pools (e.g. max 10 DB connections) or producer-consumer signaling.

Spinlock: Does not put waiting threads to sleep; repeatedly polls lock in a tight CPU loop (busy-waiting). Optimal ONLY when critical section is tiny (< few nanoseconds) where sleeping context-switch overhead exceeds spinning time.
Priority Inversion: Low-priority thread holds a mutex needed by high-priority thread, while medium-priority thread starves both. Solved via Priority Inheritance.
questions.sample_answer: A Mutex enforces strict exclusive ownership: only the thread that acquired the mutex can release it, putting waiting threads to sleep. A Semaphore is a signaling counter without ownership constraints, allowing any thread to signal; it is used to manage resource pools. A Spinlock busy-waits in a tight CPU loop instead of sleeping, making it efficient for very short critical sections where context switching would take longer than waiting. Priority Inheritance resolves Priority Inversion by temporarily elevating the low-priority thread's priority.
follow_up_questions: What is Priority Inheritance and how did it save the Mars Pathfinder mission?
Why is using a spinlock on a single-core uniprocessor machine dangerous?

questions.subtopic: CPU Scheduling Algorithms: CFS vs Round Robin
questions.question_title: How do CPU Scheduling Algorithms work: Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) vs Round Robin?
questions.question_prompt: Compare Preemptive vs Non-Preemptive scheduling. Explain Round Robin (time quantum) and Linux's default Completely Fair Scheduler (vruntime, Red-Black Tree).
expected_answer_points: Preemptive scheduling: OS scheduler can interrupt and suspend a running process to switch to another process (timer interrupts).

Round Robin (RR): Preemptive scheduler where each ready process is allocated a fixed time slice (time quantum, e.g. 10ms). Fair, but too short quantum causes high context-switch overhead, while too long degrades to FCFS.
Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS): Linux default CPU scheduler. Models an 'ideal multi-tasking CPU'.

CFS mechanism: Tracks virtual runtime (vruntime) for each task. Higher nice value (lower priority) causes vruntime to accumulate faster. Tasks are stored in a Red-Black Tree keyed by vruntime; scheduler always picks the leftmost node (task with lowest vruntime).
questions.sample_answer: Preemptive schedulers can interrupt running tasks using timer interrupts. Round Robin assigns a fixed time quantum to each task in a circular queue. The Linux kernel uses the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS): it tracks the virtual runtime (vruntime) of each thread, scaling it based on task priority (nice value). CFS stores runnable tasks in a Red-Black Tree sorted by vruntime and always picks the leftmost task (the one that has received the least CPU time), ensuring mathematically fair allocation.
follow_up_questions: What happens if the time quantum in Round Robin scheduling is set extremely small vs extremely large?
How do multi-level feedback queues (MLFQ) balance I/O-bound interactive tasks and CPU-bound batch tasks?

questions.question_title: Compare Inter-Process Communication (IPC) mechanisms in Operating Systems.
questions.question_prompt: Compare Pipes, Named Pipes (FIFOs), Message Queues, Shared Memory, and Unix Domain Sockets. Which provides the highest throughput and why?
expected_answer_points: Anonymous Pipes: Unidirectional byte stream between related parent-child processes (e.g. ls | grep).
Named Pipes (FIFO): Bidirectional communication between unrelated processes via filesystem paths.
Unix Domain Sockets: Bidirectional socket communication within the same host OS; avoids TCP/IP network stack overhead, checksums, and packet fragmentation.
Message Queues: OS-managed structured message passing.

Shared Memory: Fastest IPC mechanism. OS maps the same physical memory frame into the virtual address spaces of two different processes. Zero kernel copying (data written by Process A is instantly readable by Process B). Requires external synchronization (semaphores) to prevent race conditions.
questions.sample_answer: IPC mechanisms enable isolated processes to communicate: Pipes transfer unidirectional byte streams between related processes; Unix Domain Sockets provide bidirectional communication within a single machine without TCP/IP network stack overhead. Shared Memory is by far the fastest IPC mechanism because the OS maps the same physical memory pages into both processes' address spaces, enabling direct read/write at RAM speeds with zero kernel copying, though it requires semaphores to coordinate access.
follow_up_questions: Why are Unix Domain Sockets faster than loopback TCP network sockets (127.0.0.1)?
What system calls create and attach shared memory in Linux (shmget, shmat)?

questions.subtopic: User Space vs Kernel Space & System Calls
questions.question_title: Explain User Space vs Kernel Space and the System Call transition mechanism.
questions.question_prompt: What is Dual-Mode Operation (Ring 3 User Mode vs Ring 0 Kernel Mode)? What happens during a System Call (trap / software interrupt, register swapping, context switch)?
expected_answer_points: Dual-mode CPU protection: Hardware enforces privilege rings. Ring 3 (User Space) has restricted instruction set (cannot access hardware or memory of other processes); Ring 0 (Kernel Space) has full access to hardware and CPU registers.
System Call (syscall): Controlled programmatic gateway allowing user programs to request privileged OS services (read, write, open, fork).

Transition flow: 1) User application invokes library wrapper (e.g. glibc read()); 2) Stores syscall number and args in CPU registers; 3) Executes software interrupt/trap (syscall instruction); 4) CPU switches hardware mode from Ring 3 to Ring 0; 5) Kernel inspects System Call Table and executes driver code; 6) Switches back to Ring 3 and returns result.
questions.sample_answer: CPUs use dual-mode operation for security: User Space (Ring 3) runs applications with restricted permissions, preventing direct hardware access. Kernel Space (Ring 0) runs the OS kernel with full hardware access. When an application needs hardware I/O (like reading a file), it executes a system call (syscall). This triggers a software interrupt/trap that switches CPU execution to Ring 0, where the kernel validates parameters and executes the driver routine before switching back to Ring 3.
follow_up_questions: What is the performance overhead of transitioning between User Mode and Kernel Mode?
What is the Meltdown and Spectre CPU vulnerability regarding speculative execution and kernel memory?

questions.subtopic: Zero-Copy I/O with sendfile() and DMA
questions.question_title: How does Zero-Copy I/O work using sendfile() and Direct Memory Access (DMA)?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how standard read/write cycles require 4 context switches and 4 memory copies. How does sendfile() achieve Zero-Copy, and how do Kafka and Netty leverage it for extreme throughput?
expected_answer_points: Standard read/write cycle (4 copies, 4 context switches): 1) DMA copies data from disk to OS page cache; 2) CPU copies from page cache to user space buffer (switch to user); 3) CPU copies from user buffer to socket buffer (switch to kernel); 4) DMA copies from socket buffer to network card.
Zero-Copy sendfile() (2 copies, 2 context switches): The application calls sendfile(out_fd, in_fd).
DMA copies disk data to OS page cache. The kernel transfers file descriptors directly to socket buffer and DMA gathers data straight to the network interface card.
Zero CPU copying into user space memory; zero user-kernel context switching during data transfer.
Kafka application: Reads topic log files and streams them straight to consumer network sockets at line-rate.
questions.sample_answer: A standard file transfer involves 4 context switches and 4 data copies (including copying data back and forth into user-space application memory). Zero-Copy using the Linux sendfile() system call eliminates user-space copying entirely: the kernel reads data from disk via DMA into the OS page cache, and with Scatter-Gather DMA, transfers bytes directly from page cache to the network card buffer. Systems like Kafka and Netty use sendfile() to saturate network interfaces at line rate with almost zero CPU load.
follow_up_questions: Can Zero-Copy sendfile() be used if the application must encrypt or modify the bytes before sending?
What is mmap() (memory-mapped files) and how does it compare to sendfile()?

questions.question_title: Walk through the TCP Three-Way Handshake and Four-Way Teardown.
questions.question_prompt: Detail the sequence numbers and flags for connection setup (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and connection termination (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK). What is the TIME_WAIT state and why must it last 2MSL?
expected_answer_points: Three-Way Handshake: 1) Client -> Server: SYN (seq = x); 2) Server -> Client: SYN-ACK (seq = y, ack = x + 1); 3) Client -> Server: ACK (ack = y + 1). Establishes synchronized sequence numbers and window sizes.
Four-Way Teardown: 1) Client -> Server: FIN; 2) Server -> Client: ACK (half-closed: server can still send data); 3) Server -> Client: FIN; 4) Client -> Server: ACK.
TIME_WAIT state: The active closing party enters TIME_WAIT after sending the final ACK.
Duration: Lasts 2 * MSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime, typically 60-120 seconds).
Purpose 1: Guarantees the final ACK is received by the peer (if lost, peer re-sends FIN and client can re-ACK).
Purpose 2: Allows lingering/delayed duplicate packets from the connection to expire in the network so they don't corrupt a new connection reusing the same port pair.
questions.sample_answer: The TCP 3-way handshake establishes reliable connections: Client sends SYN, Server replies with SYN-ACK, and Client sends ACK. Connection teardown requires 4 steps: Client sends FIN, Server ACKs, Server sends its own FIN when done, and Client sends final ACK. The client then enters TIME_WAIT for 2MSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime, ~1-2 mins) to ensure the server received the final ACK and to allow all stray packets in the network to die before the IP/port tuple can be reused.
follow_up_questions: What is a SYN Flood DDoS attack and how do SYN Cookies mitigate it?
What causes a TCP Reset (RST) packet to be sent?

questions.subtopic: TCP vs UDP Comparison & Flow/Congestion Control
questions.question_title: Compare TCP and UDP: Reliability, Header Overhead, and Congestion Control.
questions.question_prompt: Why is TCP called connection-oriented and reliable, while UDP is connectionless? Explain TCP Flow Control (Sliding Window) vs Congestion Control (Slow Start, AIMD). When is UDP preferred (VoIP, DNS, QUIC/HTTP/3)?
expected_answer_points: TCP: Connection-oriented, guarantees in-order reliable delivery, retransmits lost packets, performs flow control and congestion control. Header size: 20-60 bytes.
UDP: Connectionless, unreliable, best-effort delivery, no retransmissions, no ordering guarantees, zero congestion control. Lightweight header: 8 bytes.
Flow Control: Sliding Window protocol. Receiver advertises receive window (rwnd) in headers so fast sender does not overwhelm slow receiver buffer.

Congestion Control: Prevents overwhelming intermediate network routers. Employs Slow Start (exponential window growth), Congestion Avoidance (additive increase multiplicative decrease - AIMD), and Fast Retransmit/Recovery.

UDP use cases: DNS (low latency single packet), video streaming / VoIP (dropping a frame is better than stalling video for retransmission), and HTTP/3 (QUIC uses UDP to avoid TCP head-of-line blocking).
questions.sample_answer: TCP is a connection-oriented, reliable protocol providing guaranteed in-order delivery via sequence numbers and retransmissions. It protects networks using Flow Control (receiver sliding window) and Congestion Control (Slow Start, AIMD). UDP is connectionless and lightweight (8-byte header vs 20+ for TCP) with no retransmissions or ordering. UDP is favored when low latency is critical and dropped packets are tolerable (VoIP, video calls, gaming) or for quick request-response queries like DNS.
follow_up_questions: What is Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking at the TCP layer?
How does HTTP/3 implement reliability over UDP using QUIC?

questions.question_title: How does the TLS 1.3 Handshake establish an encrypted HTTPS connection?
questions.question_prompt: Walk through the TLS 1.3 cryptographic handshake (Client Hello with Key Share, Server Hello with Certificate, Finished). How does TLS 1.3 reduce handshake latency to 1 RTT compared to TLS 1.2's 2 RTTs? What is Forward Secrecy?
expected_answer_points: Purpose: Provides Confidentiality (encryption), Integrity (HMAC), and Authentication (X.509 Certificates).
TLS 1.2: Required 2 roundtrips (2 RTT) before application data could be sent.

TLS 1.3 1-RTT Handshake: 1) Client Hello sends supported cipher suites AND client's ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key share; 2) Server Hello selects cipher, sends server key share, sends encrypted X.509 Certificate and Finished verification.
Symmetric session key is derived immediately; encrypted HTTP application data flows on the very next packet.
Forward Secrecy (PFS): Uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman keys (ECDHE). Even if the server's private RSA key is compromised years later, past recorded network traffic cannot be decrypted.
questions.sample_answer: HTTPS wraps HTTP inside TLS encryption. While TLS 1.2 required 2 round trips (2-RTT) to negotiate keys, TLS 1.3 completes the handshake in 1-RTT. The client sends its Diffie-Hellman key share in the very first ClientHello message. The server responds with its key share and encrypted certificate, allowing both sides to derive a shared symmetric session key immediately. TLS 1.3 mandates Perfect Forward Secrecy (using ephemeral ECDHE), ensuring that a future compromise of the server's private key cannot decrypt past recorded sessions.
follow_up_questions: What is TLS 0-RTT (Zero Round Trip Time) resumption and what replay attack risk does it introduce?
What is the role of a Certificate Authority (CA) in validating the server's public key?

questions.question_title: Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 protocols.
questions.question_prompt: Explain how HTTP/2 solved HTTP/1.1 head-of-line blocking using binary framing, multiplexing, and HPACK header compression. Why did HTTP/2 still suffer from TCP-level head-of-line blocking, and how does HTTP/3 (QUIC) fix it?
expected_answer_points: HTTP/1.1: Plain text protocol. Suffers from Application-layer Head-of-Line blocking (only 1 request per TCP connection at a time; browsers opened 6 concurrent TCP connections per domain to work around this).
HTTP/2: Binary framing layer. Multiplexes multiple bidirectional streams over a SINGLE TCP connection. HPACK header compression reduces bandwidth. Server Push.
HTTP/2 limitation: Because it runs over a single TCP connection, if 1 packet drops, TCP pauses ALL streams while waiting for the retransmitted packet (Transport-layer Head-of-Line blocking).
HTTP/3: Replaces TCP with QUIC over UDP. Streams are independent at the transport layer: a dropped packet on Stream 1 does NOT stall Stream 2.
0-RTT connection migration: QUIC connections survive mobile Wi-Fi to cellular switches without reconnecting.
questions.sample_answer: HTTP/1.1 suffered from application head-of-line blocking, requiring separate TCP connections for concurrent requests. HTTP/2 introduced binary framing and multiplexing, allowing hundreds of concurrent requests over a single TCP connection with HPACK header compression. However, HTTP/2 suffered from TCP-level head-of-line blocking—a single lost packet halted all multiplexed streams. HTTP/3 solves this by replacing TCP with QUIC over UDP: individual streams are isolated, so packet loss on one stream does not block others.
follow_up_questions: What is HPACK compression in HTTP/2 and how does it prevent CRIME/BREACH attacks?
What is Connection Migration in QUIC?

questions.question_title: Walk through the complete DNS Resolution process for an address like www.google.com.
questions.question_prompt: Trace a DNS query from browser cache to OS cache, recursive resolver (ISP), Root nameservers (.), TLD nameservers (.com), and Authoritative nameservers. What are A, AAAA, CNAME, and MX records?
expected_answer_points: 1. Browser checks internal DNS cache -> OS hosts file / local DNS cache.
2. Query sent to Recursive Resolver (ISP or 8.8.8.8).
3. Resolver queries Root Nameserver (.) -> returns TLD nameserver IP (.com).
4. Resolver queries TLD Nameserver (.com) -> returns Authoritative Nameserver IP (ns1.google.com).
5. Resolver queries Authoritative Nameserver -> returns A record (IPv4) or AAAA record (IPv6).
6. Resolver caches record for duration of TTL and returns IP to client browser.
Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (canonical alias), MX (mail exchange), TXT (SPF/DKIM/verification).
questions.sample_answer: DNS resolution translates hostnames to IPs. When a user requests a URL, the system checks browser and OS caches. If missing, it queries a Recursive Resolver, which performs iterative lookups: first querying the Root Nameserver (which refers to the .com TLD nameserver), then the TLD Nameserver (which refers to the domain's Authoritative Nameserver), and finally the Authoritative Nameserver, which returns the 'A' record IP address. The resolver caches the record according to its TTL and returns the IP to the browser.
follow_up_questions: What is DNS TTL (Time To Live) and what happens during DNS propagation delays?
What is DNS Spoofing / Cache Poisoning and how does DNSSEC prevent it?

questions.question_title: Compare Layer 4 (Transport) and Layer 7 (Application) Load Balancers.
questions.question_prompt: When should you use an L4 load balancer (AWS NLB, IPVS) vs an L7 load balancer (AWS ALB, Nginx, HAProxy)? Compare inspection depth, throughput, SSL termination, and routing capabilities.
expected_answer_points: Layer 4 Load Balancer: Operates at TCP/UDP transport layer. Inspects only IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports. Does not parse HTTP headers, cookies, or URLs. Ultra-high throughput (millions of requests/sec) with minimal CPU overhead.

Layer 7 Load Balancer: Operates at HTTP/HTTPS application layer. Decrypts TLS and parses HTTP methods, headers, cookies, and path URLs. Enables smart routing (e.g. /api -> backend, /images -> S3), sticky sessions via cookies, and rate limiting.
Trade-off: L4 offers raw packet-level speed; L7 offers intelligent application routing and security at higher CPU cost.
questions.sample_answer: Layer 4 load balancers operate at the transport layer (TCP/UDP), routing packets based purely on IP and port without inspecting application payloads. They achieve extreme throughput (millions of connections/sec) with minimal CPU overhead. Layer 7 load balancers operate at the application layer (HTTP/HTTPS), parsing request paths, headers, and cookies to enable intelligent routing (/api vs /static), SSL termination, and cookie-based sticky sessions at the cost of higher CPU consumption.
follow_up_questions: What is Direct Server Return (DSR) in Layer 4 load balancing?
How do Sticky Sessions work and why do they hinder even load distribution?

questions.subtopic: BSD Socket API & Blocking vs Non-Blocking I/O
questions.question_title: Explain the BSD Socket API and compare Blocking vs Non-Blocking I/O (epoll/kqueue).
questions.question_prompt: Walk through socket lifecycle system calls: socket(), bind(), listen(), accept(), connect(), send(), recv(). Why does the thread-per-connection blocking model fail to scale (C10K problem), and how does I/O multiplexing (epoll) solve it?
expected_answer_points: Lifecycle: Server: socket() -> bind(IP, port) -> listen(backlog) -> accept() [blocks until client connects] -> read()/write() -> close(). Client: socket() -> connect() -> read()/write().

C10K Problem: In thread-per-connection architectures, serving 10,000 concurrent sockets requires 10,000 OS threads. Thread stack memory (1MB per thread = 10GB RAM) and CPU context switching overhead collapse the server.
I/O Multiplexing (epoll / kqueue): A single thread monitors thousands of file descriptors. The kernel notifies the thread only when descriptors are ready for read/write (event-driven).
Forms the architectural foundation of Nginx, Node.js libuv, and Netty.
questions.sample_answer: The socket API manages network connections: servers bind, listen, and accept client connections. The legacy thread-per-connection model fails to scale (the C10K problem) because allocating an OS thread per socket exhausts RAM (1MB stack per thread) and burns CPU cycles on context switches. I/O multiplexing using Linux `epoll` solves this: a single event loop thread monitors thousands of non-blocking sockets simultaneously, waking up only when the kernel signals that a socket has data ready to read.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between Level-Triggered (LT) and Edge-Triggered (ET) epoll?
What is the listen backlog queue in TCP sockets?

questions.subtopic: Web Security: CORS, CSP, HSTS, and XSS
questions.question_title: Explain the web security triad: Same-Origin Policy (SOP), CORS, and Content-Security-Policy (CSP).
questions.question_prompt: What is the Same-Origin Policy (Protocol, Host, Port)? How does CORS relax SOP safely, and how does Content-Security-Policy (CSP) prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)? What is HSTS?
expected_answer_points: Same-Origin Policy (SOP): Browser security sandbox preventing scripts loaded from Origin A from reading DOM or network responses from Origin B unless both share identical Scheme, Host, and Port.
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): HTTP header protocol allowing servers to explicitly whitelist trusted origins (Access-Control-Allow-Origin).

CSP (Content-Security-Policy): HTTP response header instructing browsers to restrict which domains can execute scripts, styles, images, and fonts, neutralizing XSS by blocking unauthorized inline scripts and external domains.

HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security): Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains enforces that browsers communicate with the domain ONLY over HTTPS, defeating SSL stripping attacks.
questions.sample_answer: The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) prevents malicious websites from reading data from other origins unless scheme, host, and port match. CORS provides a mechanism for servers to relax SOP by sending Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers to permit cross-origin requests. Content-Security-Policy (CSP) prevents Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) by restricting where scripts can be loaded and executed from. HSTS forces browsers to connect exclusively via HTTPS, defending against man-in-the-middle SSL-stripping attacks.
follow_up_questions: What constitutes a pre-flight CORS OPTIONS request and what triggers it?
Why is 'default-src 'self'' a recommended baseline for Content-Security-Policy?

questions.question_title: Explain all five SOLID principles with concrete real-world software design examples.
questions.question_prompt: Walk through SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, and DIP. For each principle, provide a bad design that violates it and a refactored object-oriented design that adheres to it.
expected_answer_points: S - Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): A class should have one, and only one, reason to change. (Bad: OrderService computes taxes, saves to DB, and sends email. Refactor: Separate into TaxCalculator, OrderRepository, and NotificationService).

O - Open/Closed Principle (OCP): Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification. (Refactor: Use Strategy pattern or polymorphic interfaces instead of huge if/switch chains for payment types).

L - Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP): Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering correctness. (Classic violation: Square extending Rectangle where setWidth alters height, breaking client assertions).

I - Interface Segregation Principle (ISP): Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces they do not use. (Refactor: Split fat multi-method interfaces into smaller, cohesive role interfaces).

D - Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. (Refactor: Service depends on PaymentProcessor interface, not PayPalClient concrete class).
questions.sample_answer: The SOLID principles guide maintainable object-oriented architectures: Single Responsibility (classes have only one reason to change); Open/Closed (classes are open for extension via interfaces, but closed for modification); Liskov Substitution (subclasses can replace parent classes without breaking behavior); Interface Segregation (small, focused interfaces rather than bloated monolithic ones); and Dependency Inversion (high-level services depend on abstractions rather than concrete low-level implementations).
follow_up_questions: Why is the Rectangle-Square problem the classic violation of Liskov Substitution Principle?
How does Dependency Injection relate to the Dependency Inversion Principle?

questions.subtopic: Design Patterns: Factory vs Abstract Factory vs Builder
questions.question_title: Compare Factory Method, Abstract Factory, and Builder design patterns.
questions.question_prompt: When should you use Factory Method vs Abstract Factory vs Builder? How does the Builder pattern handle complex objects with dozens of optional parameters and validate immutability?
expected_answer_points: Factory Method: Defines an interface for creating a single object, deferring instantiation to subclasses.
Abstract Factory: Creates families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes (e.g. GUIFactory producing WindowsButton/WindowsCheckbox vs MacButton/MacCheckbox).
Builder Pattern: Constructs a complex object step-by-step. Separates construction from representation.

Builder benefits: Eliminates telescoping constructors with 10+ arguments, prevents parameter order bugs, allows step-by-step validation, and produces immutable objects with final fields and no setters.
questions.sample_answer: Factory Method delegates creation of a single object to subclasses. Abstract Factory provides an interface to create families of related products (like cross-platform UI controls). The Builder pattern constructs complex objects with many optional parameters step-by-step. It eliminates telescoping constructors, improves code readability via fluent APIs, and ensures thread-safe object immutability by instantiating the target object only when build() is called.
follow_up_questions: How does Joshua Bloch's static nested Builder pattern work in Java?
How does Lombok's @Builder annotation implement the builder pattern?

questions.question_title: Compare Strategy Pattern and State Pattern: Mechanics and Intent.
questions.question_prompt: Both Strategy and State patterns share similar UML class structures (composition with an interface). What is the difference in behavioral intent, client awareness, and dynamic transitions?
expected_answer_points: UML similarity: Both patterns use a Context class holding a reference to an interface with polymorphic implementations.

Strategy Pattern Intent: Swaps algorithms or behaviors. The client is typically aware of the available strategies and chooses which strategy to pass into the context (e.g. PaymentStrategy: CreditCard, PayPal, UPI).
State Pattern Intent: Encapsulates state-dependent behavior. The context changes its behavior when its internal state changes (e.g. VendingMachineState: NoMoney, HasMoney, Dispensing).

State transitions: In State pattern, state subclasses frequently know about each other and trigger transitions on the Context (e.g. HasMoneyState transitions context to DispensingState). In Strategy, strategies are independent and unaware of each other.
questions.sample_answer: While Strategy and State patterns share similar UML structures, their intent differs. In the Strategy pattern, the client explicitly selects an interchangeable algorithm to pass into the context (like choosing a sorting algorithm or payment method). In the State pattern, the context automatically alters its behavior based on its internal state machine (like a Vending Machine transitioning from NoCoin to HasCoin to Sold), and state implementations frequently manage transitions between states themselves.
follow_up_questions: How do you implement a clean finite state machine (FSM) using the State pattern in Java?
Can Strategy patterns be implemented using Java 8 Lambdas without creating explicit classes?

questions.question_title: What is the difference between the Observer Pattern and the Publish-Subscribe (Pub/Sub) Pattern?
questions.question_prompt: Explain how Observer involves direct in-memory coupling between Subject and Observers, while Pub/Sub introduces an independent Message Broker / Event Bus. Compare synchronous vs asynchronous delivery and distributed architectures.
expected_answer_points: Observer Pattern: Subject maintains a direct in-memory list of Observer references (subject.registerObserver(obs)). When state changes, Subject iterates through observers and invokes notify(). Observers and Subject are in the same process/memory space and usually synchronous.

Pub/Sub Pattern: Publishers and Subscribers NEVER know about each other (complete temporal and spatial decoupling). They communicate through an intermediary Message Broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, EventBus).
Decoupling: Publishers simply post messages to topics; subscribers subscribe to topics. Publishers do not care who, how many, or if anyone is listening.
Distributed scale: Pub/Sub works across distributed microservices; Observer is an in-process design pattern.
questions.sample_answer: In the Observer pattern, the Subject holds direct in-memory references to its Observers and notifies them synchronously within the same application process. In the Publish-Subscribe pattern, Publishers and Subscribers are completely decoupled and unaware of each other: they communicate via an intermediary Message Broker or Event Bus (like Kafka). Pub/Sub operates across distributed systems and independent processes, while Observer is an object-oriented in-process pattern.
follow_up_questions: What is the risk of memory leaks in the Observer pattern (Lapsed Listener problem)?
How does RxJava / ReactiveX combine Observer and Iterator patterns?

questions.question_title: Compare Decorator, Proxy, and Adapter structural design patterns.
questions.question_prompt: All three patterns wrap an underlying object. How do their architectural intents differ (adding behavior vs controlling access vs translating interfaces)?
expected_answer_points: Adapter: Converts the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. Resolves incompatibility between two existing interfaces without altering functionality (e.g. converting third-party legacy XML API into JSON DTO).

Decorator: Dynamically adds new responsibilities/behaviors to an object at runtime without altering its interface (e.g. Java I/O new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in))). Enhances functionality.

Proxy: Provides a surrogate or placeholder to CONTROL ACCESS to an object (e.g. Lazy initialization virtual proxy, Security proxy, Spring AOP @Transactional proxy, Remote RMI proxy). Keeps same interface; does not add business features, but controls execution.
questions.sample_answer: All three wrap an object, but their intents differ: Adapter translates an incompatible interface into an interface the client expects (interface conversion). Decorator wraps an object to dynamically add new behaviors or enhancements at runtime while keeping the same interface (like BufferedReader wrapping InputStream). Proxy wraps an object to control access, manage lazy lifecycle instantiation, or inject cross-cutting security/transaction logic without changing functionality.
follow_up_questions: How does the Java I/O stream library exemplify the Decorator pattern?
What is a Dynamic Proxy in Java (java.lang.reflect.Proxy)?

questions.question_title: Design a Multi-Level Parking Lot System (Low-Level Design).
questions.question_prompt: Design an object-oriented class model for a Parking Lot: Vehicle hierarchy (Car, Truck, Motorcycle), ParkingSpot types (Compact, Large, Motorcycle), ParkingFloor, Ticket, and ParkingRateStrategy. How do you handle concurrency when finding free spots?
expected_answer_points: Core Entities: Vehicle (abstract, licensePlate, VehicleType), ParkingSpot (spotId, SpotType, isAvailable, assignVehicle, removeVehicle), ParkingFloor (floorId, Map<SpotType, List<ParkingSpot>>), ParkingLot (singleton managing floors and entrance/exit gates).
Ticket & Payment: ParkingTicket (ticketNumber, entryTime, spotAssigned), PricingStrategy (Strategy pattern: HourlyRateStrategy, FlatRateStrategy).
Allocation algorithm: Find nearest available spot matching vehicle type using priority queues or concurrent sets.
Thread safety: Synchronized spot allocation or ConcurrentSkipListSet / ReentrantLock per floor to prevent two vehicles from being assigned the same spot simultaneously.
questions.sample_answer: Model the system with a Vehicle hierarchy (Car, Truck, Bike) and matching ParkingSpots (Compact, Large, Motorcycle). A ParkingFloor aggregates spots, and a singleton ParkingLot coordinates floors and gates. When a vehicle enters, an entrance gate finds the nearest available spot matching the vehicle type and issues a ParkingTicket recording entry time and assigned spot. Calculate fees using a PricingStrategy on exit. Use ReentrantLocks per floor or atomic boolean flags on spots to prevent double-booking under concurrent entries.
follow_up_questions: How would you support electric vehicle (EV) charging spots in this design?
How do you design for multiple simultaneous entrance and exit gates without global lock contention?

questions.question_title: Design an in-memory Rate Limiter using Token Bucket algorithm (Low-Level Design).
questions.question_prompt: Implement a thread-safe TokenBucketRateLimiter in Java: capacity, refillRate, tokens, lastRefillTimestamp. How do you refill tokens lazily without background timer threads?
expected_answer_points: Class fields: private final long capacity; private final double refillRatePerSecond; private double currentTokens; private long lastRefillTimestamp.

Lazy refill algorithm: Instead of running a background timer thread that wastes CPU, calculate tokens added lazily upon each incoming request: now = System.currentTimeMillis(); tokensToAdd = (now - lastRefillTimestamp) * refillRatePerSecond / 1000; currentTokens = min(capacity, currentTokens + tokensToAdd); lastRefillTimestamp = now.
acquire(): If currentTokens >= 1, decrement currentTokens and return true; else return false.
Concurrency: Synchronized method or ReentrantLock / AtomicReference with CAS to guarantee thread safety under concurrent requests.
questions.sample_answer: Design a TokenBucketRateLimiter class storing capacity, refill rate, current tokens, and last refill timestamp. Rather than running an expensive background timer thread, refill tokens lazily whenever tryAcquire() is called: calculate elapsed time since last request, multiply by refill rate to add tokens (capped at capacity), and update the timestamp. If at least 1 token is available, decrement and allow the request. Protect token mutations with synchronized or atomic CAS operations for thread safety.
follow_up_questions: How would you adapt this in-memory design to work across distributed servers using Redis Lua scripts?
How do you support burst capacity versus sustained rate limits in this implementation?

questions.question_title: Design a thread-safe Least Recently Used (LRU) Cache in O(1) time.
questions.question_prompt: Implement an LRUCache: get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1) time complexity. Combine a HashMap with a Doubly Linked List, and explain how to make it thread-safe.
expected_answer_points: Data structure: HashMap<K, Node> provides O(1) key lookups; Doubly Linked List maintains access recency in O(1) time.
Node structure: key, value, prev, next pointers. Dummy head and dummy tail nodes eliminate null pointer boundary checks.
get(key): If missing return -1; if present, move node to head (most recently used) and return value.
put(key, value): If key exists, update value and move to head. If new, create node, add to head, insert into map. If size > capacity, evict tail.prev (least recently used) from both list and map.
Concurrency: Wrap operations in ReentrantReadWriteLock (read lock on get, write lock on put/reorder) or synchronized block.
questions.sample_answer: Combine a HashMap for O(1) key lookups with a Doubly Linked List for O(1) removal and insertion of recency nodes. Use dummy head and tail sentinel nodes. When get(key) is called, locate the node in the map and move it to the head of the list. When put(key, val) is called, either update the existing node and move it to head, or add a new node to the head; if capacity is exceeded, evict the node immediately before the tail (LRU) from both the list and the map. Use a ReentrantLock for thread safety.
follow_up_questions: Why is a Doubly Linked List necessary instead of a Singly Linked List (O(1) deletion)?
How does Java's LinkedHashMap support LRU eviction out of the box using removeEldestEntry?

questions.question_title: Design an extensible Multi-Channel Notification Service (Low-Level Design).
questions.question_prompt: Design a notification service supporting Email, SMS, and Push Notifications: NotificationRequest, NotificationChannel strategy, TemplateEngine, Provider adapters (Twilio, SendGrid, FCM), and fallback handling.
expected_answer_points: Core interface: NotificationChannel with send(NotificationMessage).
Implementations: EmailNotificationChannel, SmsNotificationChannel, PushNotificationChannel.
Provider Adapters: SmsNotificationChannel delegates to TwilioAdapter; if Twilio fails, falls back to AWS SNS adapter (Adapter + Strategy patterns).
TemplateEngine: Resolves placeholders in templates (e.g. 'Hello {{name}}') before dispatch.
NotificationManager / Service: Asynchronously receives requests, looks up user notification preferences, and routes to appropriate channels via a Factory.
Rate Limiter & Priority Queue: Throttles outgoing SMS and prioritizes OTP verification codes over marketing blasts.
questions.sample_answer: Structure the service using the Strategy and Adapter patterns. Define a NotificationChannel interface with implementations for Email, SMS, and Push. Each channel delegates to external vendor adapters (e.g. SendGrid, Twilio) implementing a common VendorAdapter interface, enabling seamless failover if a third-party provider fails. A NotificationService pulls templates from a TemplateEngine, checks user delivery preferences, and dispatches tasks asynchronously across thread pools.
follow_up_questions: How do you design deduplication so a user never receives the same notification twice?
How do you prioritize OTP authentication messages over promotional marketing notifications?

questions.subtopic: Design a Snake and Ladder Game (LLD)
questions.question_title: Design a Snake and Ladder Board Game (Low-Level Design).
questions.question_prompt: Model Snake and Ladder using object-oriented principles: Board, Cell, Jumper (Snake/Ladder), Dice, Player, and Game controller. Walk through game loop and winning conditions.
expected_answer_points: Entities: Board (size 100, Cell[]), Cell (has optional Jumper), Jumper (start, end — if start > end it's a Snake; if start < end it's a Ladder).
Player: id, name, currentPosition.
Dice: roll() returns random integer 1-6 (or configurable N dice).
Game Controller: Queue<Player> handles turn rotation in FIFO order.

Game loop: 1) Dequeue current player; 2) Roll dice; 3) newPosition = currentPosition + roll; 4) Check board bounds (if > 100, no move); 5) Check for Jumper at newPosition and apply slide/climb; 6) If newPosition == 100, declare winner; else enqueue player.
questions.sample_answer: Model the game with Board, Cell, Jumper (encapsulating Snakes and Ladders where start > end is a snake and start < end is a ladder), Dice, and Player. The Game orchestrator maintains a FIFO Queue<Player> to manage turn order. On a turn, the player rolls the dice, updates position (staying in place if moving exceeds 100), applies any snake or ladder jump on that cell, and checks for the winning condition (reaching 100) before re-enqueuing the player.
follow_up_questions: How would you support custom rules (e.g. rolling a 6 grants another turn)?
Can a snake head land on another ladder head, and how do you prevent circular jumps during board setup?

questions.question_title: Design an In-Memory File System (Low-Level Design).
questions.question_prompt: Design an in-memory hierarchical file system: ls(path), mkdir(path), addContentToFile(path, content), and readContentFromFile(path) using a Trie/Composite pattern.
expected_answer_points: Composite pattern / Trie structure: Abstract FileSystemNode with name, parent pointer.
DirectoryNode extends FileSystemNode: Contains Map<String, FileSystemNode> children.
FileNode extends FileSystemNode: Contains StringBuilder content.
Path traversal: Split path by '/' and traverse children map step by step from root.
mkdir(path): Traverses path, creating DirectoryNodes for missing intermediate directories.
addContentToFile(path, content): Traverses to target, creates FileNode if absent, and appends content.
ls(path): If target is a file, returns file name; if directory, returns sorted list of children names.
questions.sample_answer: Use the Composite pattern where an abstract Node base class is extended by DirectoryNode (storing a Map<String, Node> of children) and FileNode (storing a StringBuilder of content). A root directory starts the tree. System methods split the input path by '/' and traverse the node map hierarchically from root. mkdir creates missing DirectoryNodes; addContentToFile appends bytes to target FileNodes; and ls() returns sorted names of directory children.
follow_up_questions: How do you implement file deletion (rm -rf) and symbolic links?
How would you ensure thread-safety for concurrent reads and writes across directory subtrees?

questions.question_title: Explain the CAP Theorem and the PACELC Theorem in distributed systems.
questions.question_prompt: Define Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Why is CA impossible in distributed networks? Explain PACELC theorem: PC/EC vs PA/EL.
expected_answer_points: CAP Theorem: In the presence of a Network Partition (P), a distributed system must choose between Consistency (C: every read receives the most recent write or an error) and Availability (A: every non-failing node returns a response without guarantee it's the latest write).
Network partitions are inevitable in real networks (cables cut, routers fail); therefore, all real distributed systems must be Partition Tolerant (CP or AP).
PACELC Theorem (extends CAP): If there is a Partition (P), trade-off between Availability (A) and Consistency (C); ELSE (E), trade-off between Latency (L) and Consistency (C).

Examples: MongoDB/HBase is PC/EC (consistent during partition, consistent in normal mode at cost of latency); DynamoDB/Cassandra is PA/EL (available during partition, low latency in normal mode with eventual consistency).
questions.sample_answer: The CAP theorem states that when a network partition occurs, a distributed system must choose between Consistency (every read returns the latest write or fails) and Availability (all requests receive responses, even if stale). Because physical network failures are inevitable, systems must be partition-tolerant (CP or AP). The PACELC theorem expands this: during Partitions, choose Availability or Consistency; ELSE, choose Latency or Consistency. Cassandra is PA/EL (eventually consistent for low latency); relational DBs are PC/EC.
follow_up_questions: What is Strong Consistency vs Eventual Consistency vs Causal Consistency?
What is the Fallacy of Distributed Computing regarding reliable networks?

questions.question_title: Compare Caching Patterns: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Write-Around, and Write-Behind.
questions.question_prompt: When should you use Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) vs Write-Through vs Write-Behind (Write-Back)? How do you prevent Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd) and Cache Penetration?
expected_answer_points: Cache-Aside: App reads from cache; if miss, reads from DB and updates cache. Writes go straight to DB and invalidate cache key. Resilient to cache failure, only caches requested data.
Write-Through: App writes to cache; cache synchronously writes to DB before returning success. Cache is always fresh, but write latency is higher.
Write-Behind (Write-Back): App writes to cache; cache acknowledges immediately and batches writes to DB asynchronously. Extreme write performance, but risks data loss on cache crash.

Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): High-concurrency key expires, causing thousands of queries to hit the database simultaneously. Fix: Distributed lock (Mutex) on cache miss or probabilistic early expiration.
Cache Penetration: Requests for non-existent keys bypass cache and hit DB. Fix: Cache null values with short TTL or use a Bloom Filter.
questions.sample_answer: Cache-Aside reads from cache, fetches from DB on miss, and writes to DB while invalidating the cache key—best for general read-heavy systems. Write-Through writes to cache and DB synchronously, ensuring fresh cache data at the cost of higher write latency. Write-Behind updates cache and writes to DB asynchronously in batches, offering extreme write throughput at the risk of data loss on crash. Mitigate Cache Stampede using distributed locks on misses, and Cache Penetration using Bloom filters.
follow_up_questions: What is Cache Avalanche and how does adding jitter to TTLs prevent it?
How does a Bloom Filter reject queries for non-existent keys before touching the database?

questions.question_title: How does Consistent Hashing work in distributed caching and database sharding?
questions.question_prompt: Why does simple hash mod (hash(key) % N) fail when nodes are added or removed? Explain the Hash Ring, virtual nodes (vnodes), and how consistent hashing limits data redistribution to K/N keys.
expected_answer_points: Problem with hash % N: If you have N=4 cache nodes and add 1 node (N=5), almost 100% of existing keys map to new nodes, causing catastrophic cache invalidation.
Hash Ring: Both server nodes and data keys are hashed using the same hash function (e.g. SHA-256) onto a 360-degree circular integer range [0, 2^32 - 1].
Lookup: Key maps to the first server node encountered moving clockwise around the ring.
Adding/Removing nodes: Only keys between the added node and its predecessor need to move (K/N keys on average); all other keys remain unaffected.
Virtual Nodes (vnodes): Each physical server is assigned multiple random positions on the ring (e.g. 100-200 vnodes per server), ensuring uniform data distribution and avoiding hot spots.
questions.sample_answer: Simple modulo hashing (hash(key) % N) causes mass cache invalidation when N changes. Consistent Hashing maps both servers and keys onto a circular hash ring [0 to 2^32 - 1]. A key is assigned to the nearest server encountered clockwise. Adding or removing a node redistributes only a fraction (1/N) of the keys between neighboring nodes. Using virtual nodes (mapping each physical server to 100+ virtual points on the ring) guarantees balanced data distribution and avoids hot spot partitions.
follow_up_questions: How does DynamoDB / Apache Cassandra use consistent hashing for data placement?
How do virtual nodes handle heterogeneous hardware servers with different RAM capacities?

questions.question_title: Design a scalable URL Shortener service (like TinyURL or Bitly).
questions.question_prompt: Design TinyURL: Capacity estimation (100M URLs/month, 10:1 read ratio), Base62 encoding vs MD5 hash truncation, Key Generation Service (KGS), database schema, and handling high-read throughput with caching.
expected_answer_points: Capacity estimation: 100M writes/month (~40 writes/sec), 10:1 read ratio (~400 reads/sec). Storage over 5 years: ~300GB.
Short link generation: Base62 encoding ([a-zA-Z0-9]). A 7-character string provides 62^7 = 3.5 trillion unique combinations.
Approach 1 (Auto-increment ID -> Base62): Simple, but sequential numbers expose business volume and require distributed coordinate counters.

Approach 2 (Key Generation Service - KGS): Standalone service pre-generates billions of unique random 7-character Base62 keys in a database, loads ranges into memory, and dispenses them instantly with zero collision risk.
Database & Caching: NoSQL Key-Value store (Cassandra, DynamoDB, or Redis) with schema { short_key (PK), original_url, created_at, user_id }. Cache hot URLs in Redis with LRU eviction.
Redirection: Return HTTP 301 (Permanent Redirect, browser caches redirection) vs 302 (Found, all clicks hit server to track analytics).
questions.sample_answer: TinyURL maps long URLs to short 7-character Base62 strings (yielding 3.5 trillion keys). A Key Generation Service (KGS) pre-generates random unique keys into a table and caches ranges in memory to hand out keys in O(1) time without collision checks. Data is stored in a key-value store (DynamoDB/Cassandra) partitioned on short_key. Hot URLs are cached in Redis to serve read traffic. Returning HTTP 302 allows tracking click analytics on every hit, while 301 reduces server load by having browsers cache the destination.
follow_up_questions: Why is HTTP 302 preferred over HTTP 301 if the business model depends on click analytics?
How do you handle link expiration and periodic cleanup of inactive URLs?

questions.question_title: How do you generate distributed unique 64-bit IDs at scale (Twitter Snowflake)?
questions.question_prompt: Why are UUIDv4 and auto-increment DB IDs unsuitable for distributed systems? Explain Twitter Snowflake: 64-bit layout (timestamp, datacenter ID, worker ID, sequence number), chronological sorting, and clock drift handling.
expected_answer_points: Why not UUIDv4: 128-bit size consumes double storage; completely non-sequential, destroying B-Tree index performance due to random disk page splits.
Why not auto-increment DB: Single point of failure, centralized bottleneck across multi-region architectures.

Snowflake 64-bit layout: 1) 1 sign bit (unused, 0); 2) 41 bits timestamp (milliseconds since custom epoch, gives ~69 years); 3) 5 bits datacenter ID (32 datacenters); 4) 5 bits worker/machine ID (32 workers per datacenter); 5) 12 bits sequence number (4,096 IDs per millisecond per machine).
Throughput: Each worker can generate up to 4 million IDs per second without network coordination.
Clock drift: If NTP synchronizes clock backwards, reject ID generation until physical time catches up.
questions.sample_answer: UUIDv4 is 128 bits and non-sequential, degrading database B-Tree index performance. Auto-increment IDs require centralized database coordination. Twitter Snowflake generates roughly time-sorted 64-bit integers locally without network coordination. The 64 bits consist of 41 bits of millisecond timestamp (69 years), 10 bits of datacenter and machine IDs (1,024 nodes), and 12 bits of local sequence counter (4,096 IDs/ms per node). Because timestamp is the highest-order component, IDs sort chronologically naturally.
follow_up_questions: What happens if NTP server synchronizes clock backward on a Snowflake generator worker?
How does UUIDv7 incorporate timestamps to solve UUIDv4 B-Tree fragmentation?

questions.subtopic: Design a Distributed Message Broker (Kafka Clone)
questions.question_title: Design a High-Throughput Distributed Message Queue.
questions.question_prompt: Architect a distributed message broker: Topic partitioning, Producer batching, Append-only commit log on disk, Consumer group offset tracking, and High Availability replication.
expected_answer_points: Core components: Broker cluster, Topics split into Partitions, Producers, Consumer Groups.
High write speed: Writes append sequentially to an immutable on-disk commit log (O(1) sequential I/O), leveraging OS page cache and bypassing random disk seeks.
High read speed: Consumers stream messages sequentially using the Zero-Copy sendfile() system call.
Scalability: Partitions are distributed across multiple brokers. Each partition has 1 Leader and N Follower replicas managed by a consensus controller (KRaft).
Offset tracking: Consumers periodically commit processed offsets to an internal topic (__consumer_offsets).
questions.sample_answer: Design a broker based on partitioned append-only commit logs. Topics are split into partitions across a broker cluster to allow horizontal scaling. Producers batch messages and write sequentially to the partition leader, which leverages OS page cache and sequential disk writes for extreme throughput. High availability is maintained by replicating partitions to follower brokers. Consumers in a consumer group read independently in order, committing their progress offsets to an internal coordinator topic.
follow_up_questions: How do In-Sync Replicas (ISR) and Leader Election work when a broker crashes?
What is the difference between RabbitMQ AMQP architecture and Kafka's pull-based consumer model?

questions.question_title: Design a Scalable Distributed Web Crawler.
questions.question_prompt: Design a distributed crawler parsing billions of web pages: URL Frontier (FIFO vs Priority queue), Politeness policies (avoiding DDoS on target domains), Duplicate detection with Bloom Filters, and distributed workers.
expected_answer_points: Components: URL Frontier, Fetcher workers, DNS Resolver cache, Content Parser, Duplicate Content Detector, Document Storage (S3/HDFS).
URL Frontier: Manages URLs to crawl. Prioritizes important pages (PageRank) and enforces Politeness (never overload a single host domain; queues URLs per host with delay intervals).
Deduplication: Web has massive duplicate links and circular loops. Use a distributed Bloom Filter or SHA-256 fingerprint hash store to check if URL/content was already crawled in O(1) time.
Robots.txt: Crawlers must parse and cache robots.txt before fetching.
Distributed scaling: Partition URLs by domain hash across a pool of stateless crawler worker pods.
questions.sample_answer: A distributed web crawler fetches and indexes billions of pages. The core component is the URL Frontier, which balances Priority (PageRank) with Politeness (queuing URLs per domain and throttling fetch rates to prevent DDoS). Crawler workers download pages using cached DNS lookups, parse out new links, and pass HTML to storage. A distributed Bloom filter checks URLs and content hashes in O(1) time to eliminate duplicate crawling and cycles.
follow_up_questions: How do you detect duplicate content when URLs differ but HTML is identical (SimHash)?
What is a Spider Trap and how do crawlers defend against infinite dynamically generated URLs?

questions.subtopic: Disaster Recovery: RTO, RPO, and Multi-Region Replication
questions.question_title: Explain Disaster Recovery planning: RTO, RPO, and Multi-Region architectures.
questions.question_prompt: Define Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO). Compare Multi-Region architectures: Active-Passive (Cold/Warm/Hot Standby) vs Active-Active. How is cross-region data replication handled?
expected_answer_points: RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Maximum acceptable duration of system downtime before service is restored.
RPO (Recovery Point Objective): Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (e.g. RPO of 5 mins means at most 5 mins of committed data can be lost in a disaster).

Active-Passive Standby: Primary region serves all traffic. Secondary region is Cold (spin up from backups), Warm (smaller capacity running), or Hot (full capacity mirroring live data). Failover requires DNS update (Route 53).

Active-Active Multi-Region: Both regions actively serve user traffic simultaneously (geo-DNS routing). Highest availability and zero RTO/RPO, but requires handling complex bi-directional cross-region database conflict resolution (CRDTs or Last-Write-Wins).
questions.sample_answer: Disaster recovery is defined by RTO (how long you can afford to be down) and RPO (how much data loss in time is acceptable). In Active-Passive, primary region serves traffic while secondary acts as a standby; failover is triggered via DNS rerouting. In Active-Active, both regions process live user requests simultaneously via Geo-DNS. While Active-Active offers near-zero RTO and lowest latency, it introduces distributed database replication lag and requires conflict resolution mechanisms for concurrent writes.
follow_up_questions: What is Split-Brain scenario during cross-region network partitions and how is quorum used to prevent it?
How does AWS Aurora Global Database achieve sub-second cross-region replication?

questions.subtopic: Design a News Feed System (Twitter / Instagram)
questions.question_title: Design a Scalable Social Media News Feed (like Twitter or Instagram).
questions.question_prompt: Compare Fan-out on Write (Push model) vs Fan-out on Read (Pull model). How do you handle the 'Celebrity / Hotspot' problem when users like Elon Musk have 100M+ followers?
expected_answer_points: Fan-out on Write (Push): When user posts, write post ID to the pre-computed news feed cache (Redis list) of ALL their followers. Reads are ultra-fast O(1) from Redis list. Disadvantage: Celebrity posting causes write explosion (1 post to 100M followers requires 100M cache updates).
Fan-out on Read (Pull): When user opens feed, pull recent posts from all followees and merge in memory. Writes are fast O(1), but reads are slow and complex for users following thousands of people.

Hybrid Model: Standard users use Fan-out on Write. Celebrities (>50k followers) use Fan-out on Read (do NOT push to followers' feeds). When a normal user opens their feed, fetch their pre-computed Redis feed and merge in recent posts from any celebrities they follow on the fly.
Feed storage: Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET) where score is post timestamp, keeping top 800 feed items in RAM.
questions.sample_answer: A News Feed system balances write and read fan-out. In Fan-out on Write (Push), a user's post is pushed into the pre-computed Redis feed of all followers, making reads instantaneous. However, this causes write bottlenecks when celebrities with 50M followers post. Production systems use a Hybrid approach: regular users push posts to followers' feeds; high-follower celebrities do not push. When a user requests their feed, the system reads their pre-computed feed and merges in recent posts from any celebrities they follow on the fly.
follow_up_questions: Why is Redis Sorted Set (ZSET) the ideal data structure for storing user timeline feeds?
How does media (image/video) upload flow asynchronously using pre-signed S3 URLs and background transcoding queues?

questions.question_title: Explain the AWS Shared Responsibility Model for Security and Compliance.
questions.question_prompt: What is AWS responsible for ('Security OF the Cloud') versus what is the Customer responsible for ('Security IN the Cloud')? Compare across IaaS (EC2), PaaS (RDS, Elastic Beanstalk), and Serverless/SaaS (S3, Lambda).
expected_answer_points: AWS Responsibility ('Security OF the Cloud'): Physical security of data centers, hardware infrastructure, virtualization hypervisors, physical networking, power, and facilities.

Customer Responsibility ('Security IN the Cloud'): Guest OS patching (on EC2), network firewall rules (Security Groups, NACLs), IAM identity and access policies, application code, data encryption at rest and in transit.

Shift with Managed Services (PaaS/Serverless): For RDS and Lambda, AWS takes over OS patching and runtime maintenance; the customer is only responsible for data, IAM permissions, and application configuration.
questions.sample_answer: The AWS Shared Responsibility Model divides security ownership: AWS owns 'Security OF the Cloud' (securing physical data centers, host hardware, cables, and virtualization hypervisors). The customer owns 'Security IN the Cloud' (managing IAM credentials, configuring security groups, encrypting sensitive data, and patching guest operating systems). With managed and serverless services like RDS or Lambda, AWS assumes responsibility for operating system and runtime patches, leaving only data and application security to the customer.
follow_up_questions: Who is responsible for encrypting customer data stored in Amazon S3?
How does the model apply to Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) control plane vs worker nodes?

questions.subtopic: AWS IAM: Users, Roles, Policies, and Least Privilege
questions.question_title: How does AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforce Least Privilege?
questions.question_prompt: Compare IAM Users, Groups, and IAM Roles. Why should EC2 instances and Lambda functions assume IAM Roles rather than storing long-lived access keys in code? How do IAM Policies evaluate allow/deny rules?
expected_answer_points: IAM User: Identity with long-term credentials (password, access key ID + secret access key). Intended for human operators.

IAM Role: Identity with NO long-term credentials. Assumed dynamically by trusted entities (EC2 instances, Lambda functions, ECS tasks) using AWS Security Token Service (STS) to obtain temporary, auto-rotating 1-hour credentials.
Security best practice: Never store static AWS access keys inside application source code, Dockerfiles, or configuration files; attach IAM Roles (Instance Profiles).
Policy evaluation: Explicit DENY always trumps any ALLOW. Default decision is implicit deny.
questions.sample_answer: IAM manages authentication and authorization in AWS. IAM Users have permanent credentials and are intended for human developers. IAM Roles have no permanent keys; they are assumed dynamically by services (like EC2 or Lambda) via AWS STS to receive temporary, automatically rotating session credentials. Applications must never hardcode access keys; instead, assign an IAM Role to the compute instance. In IAM policy evaluation, an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow, and all ungranted actions default to Deny.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between an IAM Identity-Based Policy and a Resource-Based Policy (like an S3 Bucket Policy)?
What is AWS STS AssumeRole and how is it used in cross-account access?

questions.subtopic: Core AWS Infrastructure: VPC, EC2, S3, and RDS
questions.question_title: Explain the architecture of a secure Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) in AWS.
questions.question_prompt: Design a standard multi-AZ VPC: Public Subnets (Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway) vs Private Subnets (App servers, RDS). How do Security Groups (stateful) and Network ACLs (stateless) enforce network boundaries?
expected_answer_points: VPC (Virtual Private Cloud): Isolated private virtual network in an AWS region.
Public Subnets: Have route table entry pointing to Internet Gateway (0.0.0.0/0 -> igw). Hosts internet-facing load balancers (ALB) and NAT Gateways.
Private Subnets: Have route table entry pointing to NAT Gateway for outbound internet (updates/patches), but NO public inbound IPs. Hosts backend application servers and databases.
Security Groups: Stateful virtual firewall at instance/ENI level (allowing inbound port 443 automatically allows the outbound response).
Network ACLs (NACL): Stateless subnet-level firewall with numbered allow/deny rules (requires explicit inbound AND outbound rules).
questions.sample_answer: A secure VPC spans multiple Availability Zones for high availability. Public subnets route through an Internet Gateway and host external load balancers and NAT Gateways. Private subnets have no direct public IPs and host backend microservices and databases, routing outbound traffic through the NAT Gateway. Security Groups act as stateful instance-level firewalls (allowing inbound traffic automatically allows return traffic). Network ACLs provide a stateless second layer of defense at the subnet boundary.
follow_up_questions: Why must databases like Amazon RDS always be placed in Private Subnets?
What is an AWS VPC Endpoint (PrivateLink) and how does it access S3 without traversing the public internet?

questions.subtopic: Generative AI vs Traditional Machine Learning
questions.question_title: Compare Generative AI Foundation Models with Traditional Machine Learning.
questions.question_prompt: Explain the transition from discriminative machine learning (classification, regression) to generative AI foundation models (LLMs, Diffusion). What is the Transformer architecture and self-attention mechanism?
